stem: A 44-year-old pharmacist presents with a history of recurrent episodes of faintness, sweating and tremor, occurring particularly in the late morning or late afternoon. An insulinoma is suspected. The patient is admitted for 3 days’ consecutive overnight fasting with blood glucose measurements in the morning. She remains asymptomatic during her admission and her lowest blood glucose concentration is 4.4 mmol/l. On discharge from the hospital, she reports that her symptoms have recurred. What would be the most useful investigation to establish the diagnosis?
options: Simultaneous measurement of glucose and insulin when symptomatic
Simultaneous measurement of glucose, insulin and C-peptide when symptomatic
explanation:
Simultaneous measurement of glucose, insulin and C-peptide when symptomatic
The occurrence of hypoglycaemia, other than in response to an obvious stimulus or in the fasting state, is suggestive of factitious hypoglycaemia (covert administration of insulin). In patients who are abusing exogenous insulin, insulin levels are elevated, but C-peptide is either in the normal range or suppressed.

Computed tomography pancreas
A computed tomography pancreas can be used in the investigation of an insulinoma. The absence of symptoms during a 72-hour observation period makes an insulinoma unlikely.

Measurement of glycated haemoglobin
Given the isolated episodes of hypoglycaemia, glycated haemoglobin is unlikely to be significantly reduced.

Measurement of plasma β-hydroxybutyrate
Plasma β-hydroxybutyrate concentrations tend to be low in hypoglycaemia caused by insulin (whether endogenous or exogenous: insulin suppresses lipolysis).

Simultaneous measurement of glucose and insulin when symptomatic
Measurement of insulin levels alone does not confirm whether the insulin is exogenous or endogenous.

stem: A 25-year-old man is found to have a fasting serum triglyceride concentration of 4.2 mmol/l at a routine examination for life insurance. His serum cholesterol concentration is 5.4 mmol/l; liver function tests are normal apart from a γ-glutamyltransferase activity of 114 U/l (upper limit of normal, 55 U/l), AST which is elevated at 198, (upper limit of normal is 47 U/l), and ALT is elevated at 92 U/l (upper limit of normal 50). He claims to be in good health but has a history of epilepsy for which he is taking sodium valproate. His body mass index is 24 kg/m 2. What is the most likely cause of the abnormal findings?
options: Remnant hyperlipidaemia (familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia, broad beta disease)
explanation:
Hepatic steatosis secondary to alcohol
The combination of hypertriglyceridaemia, elevated AST, and elevated γ-glutamyltransferase activity is typical of alcohol-induced hepatic steatosis.

Familial combined hyperlipidaemia
Familial combined hyperlipidaemia is incorrect. Familial combined hyperlipidaemia can cause an elevated triglyceride, cholesterol or both, but liver function tests are usually normal unless hypertriglyceridaemia is severe.

Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis
Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis is incorrect. Given the BMI is 24, NASH is less likely versus alcohol related steatohepatitis.

Remnant hyperlipidaemia (familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia, broad beta disease)
Remanant hyperlipidaemia is incorrect. Remnant hyperlipidaemia is rare, and cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations are typically much higher than in this case.

Valproate treatment
Valproate treatment is incorrect. Valproate is not an enzyme-inducing drug and does not cause an increase in γglutamyltransferase (or hypertriglyceridaemia).

stem: Antibodies to which of the following are most frequently present in the serum of patients with type 1 diabetes at diagnosis?
explanation:
Islet cell antibodies
Islet cell antibodies (usually directed against glutamic acid decarboxylase, GAD or Islet antigen-2 (IA2)) are present in the serum of patients with Type 1 diabetes at diagnosis. Although the titre may decline rapidly thereafter, persistent highly elevated titres are seen in 10-15% of patients. Memory T cells also persist which are primed for further autoimmune attack. Anti-ZnT8 antibodies, (against an intracellular component of beta cells), are also seen with accelerated beta cell failure.

Coxsackie virus
Coxsackie virus is incorrect. Antibodies to serotypes of Coxsackie virus may also be seen, and this has been suggested as a potential trigger for Type 1 diabetes. This trigger may however have been pulled some time before presentation with hyperglycaemia.

Glucagon
Glucagon is incorrect. Alpha cell function, as expressed by glucagon production is preserved for many years after the diagnosis of Type 1 diabetes.

Insulin
Insulin is incorrect. Antibodies to insulin are seen in Type 1 diabetes, but they usually appear later in the disease, are at low titre, and are often associated with use of animal insulins. Which of the following patterns of serum lipids is most characteristic of diabetes mellitus in white patients?

Cytomegalovirus
Cytomegalovirus is incorrect. There is not thought to be an association with cytomegalovirus infection and new onset Type 1 diabetes.

stem: Which of the following patterns of serum lipids is most characteristic of diabetes mellitus in white patients?
options: Elevated LDL cholesterol, elevated HDL cholesterol, elevated triglycerides
Elevated LDL cholesterol, elevated HDL cholesterol, normal triglycerides
Elevated LDL cholesterol, low HDL cholesterol, normal triglycerides
Normal LDL cholesterol, elevated HDL cholesterol, elevated triglycerides
Normal LDL cholesterol, low HDL cholesterol, elevated triglycerides
explanation:
Normal LDL cholesterol, low HDL cholesterol, elevated triglycerides
Triglycerides are most likely to be elevated in poorly controlled diabetes because of either absolute insulinopaenia or increased insulin resistance. Treatment of hyperglycaemia to achieve HbA1c within target can ameliorate much of the elevation in triglycerides.

Elevated LDL cholesterol, elevated HDL cholesterol, elevated triglycerides
Elevated LDL cholesterol, elevated HDL cholesterol, elevated triglycerides is incorrect. HDL cholesterol is most likely to be reduced in type II diabetes, and is a marker of insulin resistance.

Elevated LDL cholesterol, elevated HDL cholesterol, normal triglycerides
Elevated LDL cholesterol, elevated HDL cholesterol, normal triglycerides is incorrect. Elevated LDL and HDL cholesterol may be seen in association with SGLT-2 inhibitor therapy, although these lipid changes are not a makrer of type II diabetes per se.

Elevated LDL cholesterol, low HDL cholesterol, normal triglycerides
Elevated LDL cholesterol, low HDL cholesterol, normal triglycerides is incorrect. Isolated elevated LDL cholesterol is more likely to be seen in patients with polygenic hypercholesterolaemia.

Normal LDL cholesterol, elevated HDL cholesterol, elevated triglycerides
Normal LDL cholesterol, elevated HDL cholesterol, elevated triglycerides is incorrect. Elevated HDL cholesterol is not normally seen in type II diabetes, as low HDL cholesterol is a marker of insulin resistance. stem: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is responsible for the maintenance of normal arterial blood pressure. Many factors influence the release of aldosterone. Which of the following would increase aldosterone secretion?
explanation:
Hyponatraemia
Aldosterone is a powerful stimulant for the resorption of sodium, activating NaK pumps in the distal tubule and collecting duct, epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the collecting duct, and sodium resorption from the gut, salivary glands and sweat. Therefore, reduced levels of serum sodium will stimulate the release of renin, and in turn, the secretion of aldosterone, in order to maintain normal sodium level Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid secreted by the zona glomerulosa layer of the adrenal gland. It forms part of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Renin is secreted by the juxtaglomerular apparatus in response to hypoperfusion, hyponatraemia, or hyperkalaemia. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I. This travels in the bloodstream to the lungs, where angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) converts the angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II acts at the adrenals to stimulate the release of aldosterone. The primary actions of aldosterone are to increase sodium resorption, increase water resorption, and increase potassium loss. Its specific actions are as follows: Stimulates NaK pumps in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct of the kidney. This results in the resorption of sodium ions and the loss of potassium ions into the tubule/duct lumen. Stimulates epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the collecting duct and colon. These resorb sodium Promotes the resorption of sodium from the gut, salivary glands and sweat Stimulates the sodium chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule These three actions lead to increased water resorption, as water will follow sodium ions according to the osmotic gradient Resorption of chloride ions in addition to sodium, to maintain electrolyte balance Stimulates excretion of hydrogen ions in the collecting ducts.

Hypervolaemia
Hypervolaemia is incorrect. Renin is released in response to hypoperfusion of the juxtaglomerular apparatus in the kidney; i.e. in response to hypovolaemia. Aldosterone acts at mineralocorticoid receptors, activating NaK pumps in the distal tubule and collecting duct, epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the collecting duct, and stimulating sodium resorption from the gut, salivary and sweat glands. Consequently it is a powerful stimulus for the resorption of sodium, and therefore water, which will follow sodium ions according to the osmotic. This means that in hypervolaemia, aldosterone secretion will be reduced in order to reduce absorption of sodium and further water.

Hypokalaemia
Hypokalaemia is incorrect. Renin is released in response to raised potassium and low sodium levels. In hypokalaemia, less renin is released and therefore less aldosterone is released. Aldosterone acts at mineralocorticoid receptors to activate NaK pumps in the distal tubule and collecting duct. This results in excretion of potassium into the urine and resorption of sodium. Therefore aldosterone acts to reduce potassium levels. If the patient is hypokalaemic, then to maintain homeostasis the levels of aldosterone need to be reduced, hence hypokalaemia reduces renin and therefore aldosterone secretion.

Mean arterial pressure of 110 mmHg
Mean arterial pressure of 110 mmHg is incorrect. The mean arterial pressure (MAP) is clinically calculated as MAP ≈ DP + 1/3(SP – DP), where DP is diastolic blood pressure and SP is systolic blood pressure. This MAP corresponds to a hypertensive patient. Hypertension causes increased perfusion of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, leading to reduced renin secretion and in turn, reduced aldosterone secretion.

Taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatories
Taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, or NSAIDs, is incorrect. NSAIDs are prostaglandin inhibitors. Prostaglandins are a key part of the signalling pathway in the juxtaglomerular apparatus that eventually leads to the release of renin. Therefore as NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins, they inhibit the production of renin, and therefore the eventual secretion of aldosterone. His body mass index (BMI) is 22 kg/m 2. The fasting triglyceride concentration is 4.0 mmol/l and HbA1C is 44 mmol/mol. He has no evidence of acanthosis nigricans on examination, and blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg. There is no family history of note although he admits to drinking alcohol in excess. stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of their acidosis?
explanation:
Diarrhoea
This patient has a normal anion gap, calculated as (sodium + potassium) – (chloride + bicarbonate), which in this case equals 9.2. This is less than 11 and is therefore classified as a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Out of the options given, diarrhoea is the only cause of a normal anion gap acidosis due to bicarbonate loss.

Diabetic ketoacidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis is incorrect. This is associated with a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis, due to generation of ketoacids such as β-hydroxybutyrate.

Metformin toxicity
Metformin toxicity is incorrect. This is associated with lactic acidosis, which leads to a raised anion gap acidosis.

Methanol toxicity
Methanol toxicity is incorrect. This leads to formation of formic acid, which again leads to a raised anion gap acidosis.

Salicylate overdose
Salicylate overdose is incorrect. This is another cause of a raised anion gap acidosis.

stem: You are interested in a new gut hormone antagonist that is thought to lead to decreased hunger. Which of the following hormones is thought to stimulate hunger?
explanation:
Ghrelin
Ghrelin is secreted when the stomach is empty and drives increased hunger; levels fall once the stomach is full and remain low for approximately 3 hours after a meal. How quickly they begin to rise again may govern tendency to eat between meals and potentially drive increased consumption of high-calorie foods.

GIP
Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) is incorrect. This is an incretin hormone that increases gut transit time and may also have central effects in reducing appetite.

GLP-2
GLP-2 is incorrect. This has no significant effect on appetite, but does induce mucosal growth; it is therefore a potential target for the treatment of short bowel syndrome and radiation-induced enteritis.

Leptin
Leptin is incorrect. A rise in these levels leads to decreased appetite. A 73 year old man is referred to the Emergency Department by his GP. He has been feeling increasingly nauseous over the past few days and is known to have CKD3. His U&E are very deranged, with a potassium of 7.5 mmol/l, a creatinine of 430 micromol/l and a urea of 29.1 mmol/l. On examination his BP is 149/85 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular. He does not appear to be in fluid overload.

PYY
Peptide YY (PYY) is incorrect. Like GIP, this is an incretin, an appetite suppressant recognised to have central effects and delay gastric emptying significantly.

stem: A 73 year old man is referred to the Emergency Department by his GP. He has been feeling increasingly nauseous over the past few days and is known to have CKD3. His U&E are very deranged, with a potassium of 7.5 mmol/l, a creatinine of 430 micromol/l and a urea of 29.1 mmol/l. On examination his BP is 149/85 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular. He does not appear to be in fluid overload. Which of the following is the most effective way to rapidly reduce his potassium in this situation?
explanation:
Insulin and dextrose
This is the most effective acute intervention to reduce serum potassium: the insulin drives potassium into the intracellular space, and the dextrose prevents hypoglycaemia. Typically, 10 units of Actrapid® are given in 50ml of 50% dextrose over 15 minutes.

Calcium resonium
Tutor Calcium resonium is incorrect. This is a potassium-binding resin that will take some time to Chat reachwith AI maximal effect.

Calcium gluconate
Calcium gluconate is incorrect. While IV calcium gluconate is of course indicated under cardiac monitoring in this situation, its role is cardioprotective rather than the actual reduction of serum potassium.

Furosemide
Furosemide is incorrect. Given that the creatinine is 430 mcmol/l, this is not particularly effective as a diuretic, even when given at high dose.

Salbutamol
Salbutamol is incorrect. Although it may have additive effects on reducing potassium, and can be given concurrently with insulin and dextrose, it may be pro-arrhythmogenic.

stem: Which of the following would you consider the most likely risk factor for this man’s osteoporosis?
explanation:
Low testosterone
The long-term period of low libido, coupled with a fracture some 3 years earlier, raises the possibility of hypogonadism; low testosterone should therefore be considered a significant possible risk factor for osteoporosis in this case.

Alcohol consumption
Alcohol consumption is incorrect. Haemoglobin and platelets are normal here, both of which count against significant alcohol consumption.

Elevated BMI
Elevated BMI is incorrect. In the absence of diabetes, this is associated with increased bone mineral density.

Low normal calcium
Low-normal calcium is incorrect. This patient’s calcium at 2.15 mmol/l is not associated with increased risk of bone fracture, especially given the normal alkaline phosphatase.

Smoking history
Smoking history is incorrect. Although cigarette smoking is strongly associated with osteoporosis, an occasional cigar will not significantly impact on his bone mineral density.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Milk–alkali syndrome
Although milk–alkali syndrome is now rare, given the easy availability of both H2 antagonists and proton pump inhibitors, it is occasionally seen, particularly in patients who purchase over-the-counter calcium carbonate- or magnesium hydroxide-type preparations.

Multiple myeloma
Multiple myeloma is incorrect. Lab tests are entirely normal apart from calcium, which counts against multiple myeloma, particularly with respect to the normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

Occult carcinoma
Occult carcinoma is incorrect. The lack of anaemia, abnormal liver function tests or abnormal alkaline phosphatase counts against occult carcinoma.

Paget’s disease
Paget’s disease is incorrect. This is associated with a normal calcium and an elevated alkaline phosphatase.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. This is associated with elevated calcium and an elevated alkaline phosphatase.

stem: A 42-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of lethargy and tiredness. His urine tested positive for glucose, and a random blood glucose concentration was 8.3 mmol/l. An oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) revealed: glucose concentration at baseline at 5.6 mmol/l, rising to 9.3 mmol/l at 120 minutes. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The combination of the random glucose and glycosuria are diagnostic of diabetes
The result of the OGTT confirms a diagnosis of diabetes
The result of the OGTT confirms a diagnosis of impaired fasting glucose by WHO criteria
The result of the OGTT indicates impaired glucose tolerance
The result of the OGTT indicates that he is at significant increased risk of microvascular disease
explanation:
The result of the OGTT indicates impaired glucose tolerance
The combination of a fasting venous plasma glucose concentration of <7.0 mmol/l and a 2-hour value of 7.8 mmol/l or greater but <11.1 mmol/l is diagnostic of impaired glucose tolerance.

The combination of the random glucose and glycosuria are diagnostic of diabetes
The combination of the random glucose and glycosuria are diagnostic of diabetes is incorrect. Random glucose values should not be used to diagnose diabetes mellitus and glucosuria can of course occur in patients with naturally occurring SGLT-2 mutations who have familial glycosuria in the presence of normal serum blood glucose levels.

The result of the OGTT confirms a diagnosis of diabetes
The result of the OGTT confirms a diagnosis of diabetes is incorrect. The fasting glucose is below the limit for a diagnosis of diabetes, as is the 2-hour glucose value.

The result of the OGTT confirms a diagnosis of impaired fasting glucose by WHO criteria
The result of the OGTT confirms a diagnosis of impaired fasting glucose is incorrect. Impaired fasting glucose is defined by WHO criteria as a fasting plasma glucose between 6.1 and 6.9 mmol/l.

The result of the OGTT indicates that he is at significant increased risk of microvascular disease
The result of the OGTT indicates that he is at significant increased risk of microvascular disease is incorrect. The risk of microvascular disease only rises significantly once blood glucose enters the diabetic range.

stem: A 42-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus, which was diagnosed 23 years ago, is admitted to hospital with diabetic ketoacidosis. He is complaining of abdominal pain and has vomited a number of times.On examination his temperature is 38.0°C, BP is 100/70 mmHg, pulse is 100/min and regular. His respiratory rate is elevated at 30. Which of the following findings on admission would most suggest an identifiable acute event has precipitated his diabetic ketoacidosis?
options: Serum amylase activity of 1244 μ/l (upper limit of normal, 150 μ/l)
explanation:
Serum amylase activity of 1244 μ/l (upper limit of normal, 150 μ/l)
Although patients with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) often have elevated serum amylase, the magnitude of elevation to approximately nine times the upper limit of normal suggests underlying acute pancreatitis as a precipitant for the event.

Serum creatinine concentration 140 μmol/l
Serum creatinine concentration 140 μmol/l is incorrect. A degree of pre-kidney disease due to volume depletion associated with ketoacidosis is common.

Serum lactate concentration 4.3 mmol/l
Serum lactate concentration 4.3 mmol/l is incorrect. Lactate may be elevated in patients with DKA as a result of poor tissue perfusion although this is not invariably the case.

Serum triglyceride concentration 5.2 mmol/l
Serum triglyceride concentration 5.2 mmol/l is incorrect. Hypertriglyceridaemia is common in uncontrolled diabetes, but levels of 5.2 would be unlikely to be a driver for acute pancreatitis. 4

White cell count of 15 × 10 9/l
White cell count of 15 × 10 9/l is incorrect. An elevated white cell count is common in patients presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis.

stem: In a patient with chronic hyponatraemia (sodium concentration 112 mmol/l), who has plasma glucose of 7.5 mmol/l and serum urea of 3.1 mmol/l, which of the following findings would most suggest a diagnosis of the syndrome of inappropriate (secretion of) antidiuretic hormone (SIADH)?
explanation:
Urinary osmolality 350 mosmol/kg
The most significant finding in this patient is that the urine is concentrated relative to plasma; this is inappropriate, in that a low plasma osmolality should suppress antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion and lead to the formation of a maximally dilute urine.

Normal cortisol response to ACTH
Normal cortisol response to ACTH is incorrect. The normal cortisol response to ACTH is merely used to exclude a diagnosis of Addison’s, rather than to confirm a diagnosis of SIADH.

Plasma albumin concentration 28 g/l
Plasma albumin concentration 28 g/l is incorrect. Plasma albumin concentration 28 g/l suggests another potential cause of hyponatraemia such as liver or kidney failure.

Plasma osmolality 248 mosmol/kg
Plasma osmolality 248 mosmol/kg is incorrect. The low plasma osmolality reflects the hyponatraemia, since sodium is the principal determinant of extracellular fluid osmolality. It does not reveal information as to the underlying cause.

Urinary sodium concentration <20 mmol/l
Urine sodium concentration<20 mmol/l is incorrect. A low urine sodium excretion would suggest extrarenal sodium depletion as a cause of hyponatraemia.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes being treated with a thiazide and a beta-blocker for hypertension is found to have a serum potassium concentration of 3.2 mmol/l. Her blood pressure is 156/94 mmHg; serum creatinine concentration is 115 μmol/l. What is the most likely cause of the hypokalaemia?
explanation:
The thiazide diuretic
Loop and thiazide diuretics increase sodium delivery to the distal segment of the distal tubule; this increases potassium loss because the resultant increase in distal tubular sodium concentration stimulates the aldosterone-sensitive sodium pump, increasing sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions, which are then lost in the urine. Thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide are less likely versus traditional thiazides such as bendroflumethiazide to lead to hypokalaemia.

Low dietary potassium intake
Low dietary potassium intake is incorrect. Most people have an adequate dietary potassium intake; a low potassium diet requires significant changes to food groups consumed, and is associated with significant palatability issues.

Primary aldosteronism
Primary aldosteronism is incorrect. Although primary hyperaldosteronism is a possibility, thiazide-related hypokalaemia should be excluded first by changing the thiazide for an alternative agent.

Renal tubular acidosis type 4
Renal tubular acidosis type 4 is incorrect. Whereas renal tubular acidoses types 1 and 2 are associated with hypokalaemia, type 4 (hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, most frequently seen in patients with diabetes) is associated with hyperkalaemia.

The beta-blocker
The beta-blocker is incorrect. Non-selective beta blockade is recognised to impair entry of potassium into cells, leading to hyperkalaemia rather than hypokalaemia.

stem: Her potassium concentration has risen over the past 3 days. The potassium content of the parenteral feed has been reduced from 60 mmol/24 h to 20 mmol/24 h during this period. Urine output is appropriate to her fluid input. Her red cell, white cell and platelet counts are all normal. What is the most likely cause of the hyperkalaemia?
options: Overprovision of potassium in the parenteral feed
explanation:
Heparin treatment
Heparin inhibits aldosterone secretion by the adrenal cortex, leading to impaired renal potassium excretion, particularly in patients with diabetes or those who are acidotic.

Overprovision of potassium in the parenteral feed
Overprovision of potassium in the parenteral feed is incorrect. Approximately 20 mmol/24 h is the minimum obligatory potassium output, while the typical potassium requirement for patients on parenteral feeding is 40– 80 mmol/24 h. Partial resection of small intestine is likely to drive excess potassium loss, and parenteral feeding is very well controlled, making iatrogenic hyperkalaemia very unlikely.

Primary adrenal failure (Addison’s disease)
Primary adrenal failiure (Addison's disease) is incorrect. Adrenal failure is more likely to be associated with type 1, rather than type 2, diabetes, and an additional pathology would be unlikely on top of heparin as a reason for the hyperkalaemia.

Pseudohyperkalaemia
Pseudohyperkalaemia is incorrect. Pseudohyperkalaemia is hyperkalaemia occurring as a result of a loss of potassium from white cells and platelets during clotting, usually seen in patients with high white cell or platelet counts, or from defects in blood taking technique, driving collection of a haemolysed sample.

Renal impairment
Renal impairment is incorrect. The creatinine is 120 μmol/l, which counts against a diagnosis of kidney disease here. The elevated urea may be related to excess provision of amino acids.

stem: A 54-year-old man with a long history of excessive alcohol ingestion develops a blistering skin eruption. His urine tests positive for porphyrins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda
Cutaneous hepatic porphyria (porphyria cutanea tarda) can be inherited in autosomal dominant fashion, but is more frequently acquired (80% of cases), and is seen most frequently in association with excessive alcohol intake, with or without liver disease. It is due to a deficiency in activity of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD). High factor sun screens are essential, tobacco smoking is not advised, oestrogens should be discontinued in women who have the condition, and alcohol should be stringently avoided. Symptoms usually slowly resolve once alcohol is discontinued.

Acute intermittent porphyria
Acute intermittent porphyria is incorrect. Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is an acute porphyria associated with abdominal pain, hypertension and tachycardia, and also features neuropsychiatric symptoms. Skin rash is not a feature of AIP. AIP is due to deficient activity of porphobilinogen deaminase.

Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria
Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria is incorrect. Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria is associated with a double gene deficiency with respect to production of UROD, and leads to a much earlier presentation with similar symptoms to porphyria cutanea tarda, without excess alcohol consumption.

Hereditary coproporphyria
Hereditary coproporphyria is incorrect. Hereditary coproporphyria is due to deficient action of coproporphyrinogen oxidase, and similar to AIP is an acute porphyria. In an adult patient with cirrhosis, which of the following findings is the most reliable diagnostic indicator that hereditary haemochromatosis is the cause of his underlying condition?

Variegate porphyria
Variegate porphyria is incorrect. Variegate porphyria is characterised by both acute attacks and photosensitisation, is less common than cutaneous hepatic porphyria, and is always genetically determined. It is due to a deficiency in protoporphyrinogen oxidase activity.

stem: You are asked to review a 60-year-old man who is being treated for postoperative ileus following colectomy and has a nasogastric tube in place. This has aspirated a considerable volume of gastric fluid. He has a metabolic alkalosis What is the most important cause of the acid–base disturbance?
explanation:
Loss of gastric acid
Loss of unbuffered gastric acid causes metabolic alkalosis in prolonged nasogastric aspiration in postoperative ileus if there is inadequate replacement of fluid loss with intravenous physiological saline. The alkalosis is maintained by increased renal bicarbonate reabsorption and potassium depletion, at least in part driven by a secondary increase in aldosterone.

Hypoventilation
Hypoventilation is incorrect. Hypoventilation is a compensatory change in response to the metabolic alkalosis; on its own, hypoventilation causes carbon dioxide retention and a respiratory acidosis.

Increased renal bicarbonate reabsorption
Increased renal bicarbonate reabsorption is incorrect. The increased renal bicarbonate reabsorption andTutor hydrogen ion loss occur as a result of secondary increase in aldosterone because of volume loss.

Potassium depletion
Potassium depletion is incorrect. Potassium depletion occurs as a result of prolonged vomiting and is not the direct cause of the metabolic alkalosis.

Secondary aldosteronism
Secondary aldosteronism is incorrect. The increase in aldosterone occurs as a result of the vomiting and volume depletion, it is not the primary cause of the metabolic alkalosis.

stem: A 75-year-old man with symptoms of prostatism over the last 5–6 months comes to the clinic for review. Abdominal examination is unremarkable, he has no renal masses and does not have a palpable bladder. PR is unremarkable. He has a serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) concentration of 7.0 ng/ml, and his creatinine is 150 μmol/l. Which of the following statements is true with regard to this result?
options: It could be explained by prostatitis
It is likely to be invalid if he had undergone a digital rectal examination 48 hours before the blood
It is unremarkable in a man of this age
explanation:
It could be explained by prostatitis
Prostatitis and acute urinary retention can both result in increased serum concentrations of PSA. This patient has been suffering from symptoms of prostatism for more than three months. In chronic bacterial prostatitis, physical exam, including PR, is often normal. Hence, chronic prostatis is the most likely option.

It is diagnostic of malignancy
It is diagnostic of malignancy is incorrect. A PSA level of 7 ng/ml is certainly compatible with malignancy, but is not diagnostic of it. Lower levels of PSA are seen in patients with benign prostatic hypertrophy and with prostatitis.

It is likely to be invalid if he had undergone a digital rectal examination 48 hours before the blood
It is likely to be invalid if he had undergone a digital rectal examination 48 hours before the blood sample was taken Some authors believe that PSA should not be measured after a DRE. However, clinical studies have shown that the elevation in PSA levels is clinically insignificant and therefore this should not invalidate the result.

It is prognostically highly significant
It is prognostically highly significant is incorrect. In general, the higher the PSA, the greater the likelihood of malignancy, but some patients with malignancy have normal levels, because they have an underlying tumour which does not produce PSA. The absolute PSA concentration correlates poorly with prognosis in prostatic cancer, particularly where elevated levels have been identified at diagnosis.

It is unremarkable in a man of this age
It is unremarkable in a man of his age is incorrect. An upper limit of normal for PSA of 0–4 ng/ml is usually applied to results, although this is adjusted up slightly with increasing age. A value of 7 ng/ml would definitely be considered abnormal.

stem: What would be the most important therapeutic measure?
explanation:
Intravenous infusion of desferrioxamine
The most important intervention in this situation, with a very high level of serum iron, is chelation therapy, facilitating its urinary excretion. It is most effective given as a continuous infusion, approximately 8 mg of iron is bound by 100 mg of desferrioxamine.

Gastric lavage with enteral desferrioxamine
Gastric lavage with desferrioxamine is incorrect. Serum iron is already approaching highly toxic levels, as such although instilling desferrioxamine into the GI tract may drive some iron chelation, it is not likely to be effective in avoiding complications of iron overdose.

Induction of vomiting
Induction of vomiting is incorrect.The induction of vomiting is ineffective if carried out more than 1 hour after ingestion and iron toxicity itself often causes vomiting.

Oral activated charcoal
Oral activated charcoal is incorrect. Activated charcoal poorly adsorbs inorganic poisons such as iron. You are called by the ambulance service for a pre-alert about a 22-year-old woman who has taken two full bottles of aspirin 300 mg tablets some 2 hours earlier. What clinical feature on arrival would most suggest that another drug has been taken in addition to aspirin?

Whole bowel irrigation
Whole bowel irrigation is incorrect. Whole bowel irrigation may be helpful if undissolved tablets remain in the gut, as is more likely to occur when slow-release iron preparations have been ingested. It is an additional therapy to desferrioxamine however, rather than an alternative to it.

stem: You are called by the ambulance service for a pre-alert about a 22-year-old woman who has taken two full bottles of aspirin 300 mg tablets some 2 hours earlier. What clinical feature on arrival would most suggest that another drug has been taken in addition to aspirin?
explanation:
Coma
Although decreased consciousness is seen in aspirin overdose, it is seen late, and is associated with severe metabolic acidosis and hypokalaemia.

Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation is incorrect. Hyperventilation is the most prominent feature of the early period after aspirin overdose, and is associated with respiratory alkalosis.

Sweating
Sweating is incorrect. Sweating with peripheral vasodilatation and a bounding pulse is a common feature of aspirin overdose.

Tinnitus
Tinnitus is incorrect. Tinnitus is a common feature of aspirin overdose, and is related to activation of cochlear NDMA receptors. Fluid Balance and Fluid Replacement Therapy

Vomiting
Vomiting is incorrect. Gastric irritation, including vomiting, is commonly seen in pateints with aspirin overdose.

stem: Which of the following drugs is he most likely to have taken?
explanation:
Theophylline
The blood gas data in this patient indicate an acute respiratory alkalosis, which is particularly associated with poisoning with a salicylate and theophylline, both of which are respiratory stimulants. Seizures are common in theophylline overdose and are usually managed with benzodiazepines. Very large amounts of potassium supplementation may be required to manage hypokalaemia associated with theophylline overdose.

A benzodiazepine
A benzodiazepine is incorrect. Benzodiazepines are respiratory depressants, leading to respiratory acidosis rather than alkalosis.

A tricyclic antidepressant
A tricyclic antidepressant is incorrect. Tricyclic antidepressants in overdose are associated with significant respiratory depression, coma and fits.

Cocaine
Cocaine is incorrect. Cocaine causes tachycardia, hypertension and anxiety, and may in chronic use lead to accelerated ischaemic heart disease, but it does not usually result in such severe hyperventilation that a pH of 7.56 is achieved.

Paracetamol (acetaminophen)
Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is incorrect. Significant acid–base disturbance is seen late in paracetamol overdose, and metabolic acidosis is the usual prominent feature.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is admitted to the surgical unit with an episode of moderate to severe acute pancreatitis who has eaten little over the last 24 hours due to severe nausea. You are asked to give an opinion as to the best way to meet her nutritional needs. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial way to manage them?
explanation:
Nasogastric feeding
Studies have shown that continuing feeding in acute pancreatitis rather than moving to a nil by mouth state is the best way to maintain integrity of the gastrointestinal tract with respect to potential bacterial invasion. Nasogastric (NG) feeding is the default initial choice, and if vomiting persists/there is significant gastric stasis, alternative such as nasojejunal feeding should be considered before moving to parenteral feeding.

Continue oral intake
Continue oral intake is incorrect. Maintaining adequate calorie intake is crucial with respect to outcomes in acute pancreatitis; it is unlikely that a patient with acute pancreatitis will be able to maintain adequate calorie intake without supplemental NG feeding.

Nasojejunal feeding
Nasojejunal feeding is incorrect. Nasojejunal feeding is the default alternative option if NG feeding is not tolerated due to persistent vomiting.

Nil by mouth for 48 hours
Nil by mouth for 48 hours is incorrect. Nil by mouth for 48 hours could potentially lead to significant calorie deficit and worse outcomes in acute pancreatitis with respect to increased time in a high-dependency hospital setting, and increased 60-day mortality. 7 27 You are asked to review a 71-year-old patient who has received excess blood transfusions and saline fluid replacement after a bleed following left total hip replacement. You estimate that approximately a 20% increase in his blood volume has occurred. What physiological process is most likely to correct this abnormality?

Parenteral feeding
Parenteral feeding is incorrect. Parenteral feeding is only considered if both NG and nasojejunal feeding are not tolerated, as it does not ameliorate the risk of small bowel perforation associated with pancreatitis.

stem: A 16-year-old teenager has suffered recurrent haemarthroses affecting both knees after playing sports, and a bleeding episode after dental extraction. As a consequence of the haemarthroses he has arthritis affecting both knees. Only male members of his family have been affected by the bleeding tendency, and his APTT is prolonged on coagulation testing. What is the most likely coagulation factor deficiency causing his bleeding tendency?
explanation:
Factor VIII
Deficiency of either factor VIII (haemophilia A) or factor IX (haemophilia B), which together make up the factor VIIIa/factor IXa intrinsic tenase enzymatic complex, results in the development of haemophilia. The pathological problem in both haemophilia A and haemophilia B (also called “Christmas disease”) is the inability to form a functional tenase complex to activate factor X to factor Xa. The disease exists in severe, moderate and mild forms. These are classified as such on the basis of a clinical laboratory blood coagulation test, which is performed to assess the level of functional coagulant protein (percentage activity of factor VIII in haemophilia A or factor IX in haemophilia B). In mild disease patients may present relatively late in life with joint haemorrhage or bleeding after dental extraction. The condition is Xlinked, accounting for the inheritance pattern seen here.

Protein C
Protein C is incorrect. Protein C deficiency results in increased propensity to clot/form venous thromboses, rather than bleeding episodes.

Protein S
Protein S is incorrect. Protein S deficiency, like protein C deficiency, results in increased propensity to clot/form venous thromboses, rather than bleeding episodes.

Thromboxane
Thromboxane is incorrect. Thromboxane synthetase deficiency does lead to abnormal platelet function and increased bleeding tendency, but it follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. 7 30 You are asked to assess the cardiovascular risk status of a man with impaired glucose tolerance and severe obesity. You suspect he is highly insulin resistant. Which of the following pathophysiological changes is most strongly associated with increased insulin resistance?

von Willebrand factor
von Willebrand factor is incorrect. von Willebrand’s disease does present with haemoarthrosis and prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), but it is mostly inherited in autosomal dominant fashion.

stem: You are asked to assess the cardiovascular risk status of a man with impaired glucose tolerance and severe obesity. You suspect he is highly insulin resistant. Which of the following pathophysiological changes is most strongly associated with increased insulin resistance?
options: Increased levels of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1
explanation:
Increased levels of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1
Insulin resistance is associated with a procoagulant state, driven at least in part by increased levels of PAI-1, which in itself is a risk factor for myocardial infarction.

Decreased platelet aggregation
Decreased platelet aggregation is incorrect. Both ICAM and VCAM-1 levels are thought to be increased in patients who are insulin resistant, driving increased propensity for platelet adhesion to occur.

Hypotension
Hypotension is incorrect. Hypotension Insulin resistance is associated with hypertension, both driven by obesity and by higher circulating insulin driving increased sodium and water retention.

Improved endothelial function
Improved endothelial function is incorrect. Increased blood pressure and vascular inflammation may well be responsible for driving a deterioration in endothelial function in patients with insulin resistance.

Increased HDL levels
Increased HDL levels is incorrect. Patients with high levels of insulin resistance have an atherogenic lipid profile as evidenced by low HDL cholesterol and elevated triglycerides.

stem: An 81-year-old nursing-home resident is admitted to hospital in an unconscious state. His blood sugar is measured as 1.5 mmol/l (normal 3–6 mmol/l). You administer glucagon. Which of the following best describes one of the main actions of glucagon?
options: Decreased ketone body production from fatty acids
explanation:
Increased glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
Glucagon is produced by alpha cells which are found in pancreatic islets. Its main action is on the liver to promote glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

Decreased gluconeogenesis
Decreased gluconeogenesis is incorrect. Gluconeogenesis, the production of glucose from alternative noncarbohydrate carbon sources such as lactate and glycerol is promoted by glucagon action.

Decreased glycogenolysis
Decreased glycogenolysis is incorrect. Glucagon’s role is to maximise energy mobilisation from stores, including from glycogen.

Decreased ketone body production from fatty acids
Decreased ketone body production from fatty acids is incorrect. Glucagon promotes fatty acid oxidation, which leads to an increase in ketones such as beta hydroxybutyrate.

Increased lipogenesis in adipose tissue
Increased lipogenesis in adipose tissue is incorrect. The actions of glucagon on adipose tissue are mediated by cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP) to stimulate lipolysis, producing free fatty acids that can act as a major alternative energy source. You are reviewing a man with familial hypertriglyceridaemia who has presented to the surgeons with pancreatitis. He asks about why he suffers from this condition.

stem: You are reviewing a man with familial hypertriglyceridaemia who has presented to the surgeons with pancreatitis. He asks about why he suffers from this condition. Which of the following best describes the metabolism of VLDL (predominant triglyceride) particles?
options: They are formed from IDL particles
They are synthesised continuously in the liver
They are synthesised postprandially in the small intestine
They bind primarily to the hepatic LDL receptor
They take up cholesterol from cells
explanation:
They are synthesised continuously in the liver
Most familial hypertriglyceridaemia is polygenic in origin, and due to a modest excess in the circulating concentration of very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) particles. There may be a history of retinal vein thrombosis or recurrent pancreatitis in individuals affected by the familial condition who have very high triglyceride levels (>11 mmol/l). VLDL particles are synthesised continuously in the liver and contain most of the triglyceride the body produces and a smaller amount of cholesterol. They provide the main source of energy during prolonged periods of fasting. They have apolipoprotein C-II on their surface, which has the following consequences: it allows them to bind to capillary endothelium it allows for triglycerides to be progressively removed by lipoprotein lipase, which leaves a particle depleted of triglyceride and apolipoprotein C-II, known as an IDL (intermediate-density lipoprotein) particle.

They are formed from IDL particles
They are formed from IDL particles is incorrect. IDL particles are metabolised to form particles of LDL cholesterol.

They are synthesised postprandially in the small intestine
They are synthesised postprandially in the small intestine is incorrect. Chylomicrons are synthesised postprandially in small intestinal enterocytes.

They bind primarily to the hepatic LDL receptor
They bind primarily to the hepatic LDL receptor is incorrect. The hepatic LDL receptor is primarily there to recognise LDL cholesterol, although some VLDL is recognised by the hepatic LDL receptor because of the Apo E moiety.

They take up cholesterol from cells
They take up cholesterol from cells is incorrect. The primary function of HDL is to take up cholesterol from cells.

stem: You suspect Cushing’s disease. He refuses to comply with urine collection but will consent to a blood test for cortisol. At what time of day is a random cortisol test most likely to be abnormal?
explanation:
2400 hours
Plasma cortisol levels in normal individuals show a circadian rhythm. Levels are highest in the early morning, and fall to their lowest levels during sleep at around midnight. In patients with Cushing’s syndrome, the 0900 hours cortisol level may be within the normal range, but midnight levels are usually not suppressed. Isolated venous blood tests for cortisol levels are not the best way to detect Cushing’s syndrome. A 24-hour urine collection with analysis of cortisol levels is a much better early screening test for Cushing’s syndrome. Melatonin follows the opposite pattern to cortisol with levels being highest during periods of sleep.

0900 hours
0900 hours is incorrect. In normal individuals cortisol levels are highest at around 0900 hours, and during this time period they may be in the normal range in patients with Cushing’s.

1200 hours
1200 hours is incorrect. Levels of cortisol during the day are not useful with respect to predicting risk of Cushing’s.

1700 hours
1700 hours is incorrect. Similar to looking at levels at 1200 hours, levels of cortisol during the peak period of activity are not useful in differentiating Cushing’s from normal individuals. You are asked to review a 45-year-old obese woman who is jaundiced; you suspect that she may have primary biliary cirrhosis with accumulation of bile salts.

2000 hours
2000 hours is incorrect. Although levels are beginning to tail off by 2000 hours, if an isolated venous sample for Cushing’s is the only option, waiting until later in the evening is recommended.

stem: You are asked to review a 45-year-old obese woman who is jaundiced; you suspect that she may have primary biliary cirrhosis with accumulation of bile salts. Which of the following best fits the metabolism of bile acids?
options: Around 30% of the bile acid pool is lost in faeces each day
Concentration in the gall bladder is around 500 mmol/l
The total bile salt pool in the liver is around 10 g
Their production is catalysed by cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase
80% of bile salts are reabsorbed during each cycle
explanation:
Their production is catalysed by cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase
Bile salts are synthesised in hepatocytes from cholesterol via a process catalysed by cholesterol 7αhydroxylase. They are then excreted in bile and pass into the duodenum.

Around 30% of the bile acid pool is lost in faeces each day
Around 30% of the bile acid pool is lost in faeces each day is incorrect. Total faecal loss is around 10–20% of the bile acid pool in any one day. Intestinal bile acid transport inhibitors which promote faecal loss of bile acids are a target in the treatment of type 2 diabetes and primary biliary cirrhosis.

Concentration in the gall bladder is around 500 mmol/l
Concentration in the gall bladder is around 500 mmol/l is incorrect. Bile acids exist in the gall bladder at a concentration of between 100 and 300 mmol/l. The two primary bile acids (cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid) them Tutor into are conjugated with glycine or taurine which increases their solubility. Intestinal bacteria then convert secondary bile acids.

The total bile salt pool in the liver is around 10 g
The total bile salt pool in the liver is around 10 g is incorrect. The total bile salt pool in the liver is small at around 2.5–5g.

80% of bile salts are reabsorbed during each cycle
80% of bile salts are reabsorbed during each cycle is incorrect. The enterohepatic circulation ensures the bile salt pool is recycled 6–8 times per day, leading to reabsorption of 80-90% of bile acids.

stem: A 55-year-old chronic heavy smoker is brought to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of polyuria, polydipsia, nausea and progressive drowsiness. On examination, he is lethargic and confused. A chest radiograph shows a round shadow in the right mid-zone with enlarged hilar lymph nodes on the right side. An ECG is normal except for a narrowed QT interval and notching of the terminal portion of the QRS most prominent in V1. What is the most likely metabolic abnormality in this case?
explanation:
Hypercalcaemia
The ECG features with notching of the QRS and a narrowing of the QT interval are typical features of hypercalcaemia, as is the polyuria, polydipsia and progressive drowsiness described in his history. An underlying bronchial squamous cell carcinoma is the most likely cause.

Hyperkalaemia
Hyperkalaemia is incorrect. Hyperkalaemia is associated with peaked T waves, and with higher levels of potassium, progressive widening of P waves and lengthening of the PR interval.

Hypernatraemia
Hypernatraemia is incorrect. Hypernatraemia is associated with the symptoms described, although it is much more commonly seen in the elderly following a cerebral event, and is not associated with the ECG changes seen here.

Hyperphosphataemia
Hyperphosphataemia is incorrect. In the event that the hypercalcaemia seen here is related to PTH-related peptide, hypophosphataemia, rather than high levels of phosphate, are likely here.

Hypokalaemia
Hypokalaemia is incorrect. Hypokalaemia is associated with T-wave flattening, ST depression, and U waves seen on the ECG.

stem: Antimitochondrial and anti-smooth muscle antibodies are positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
explanation:
Primary biliary cholangitis
The high alkaline phosphatase concentration in this patient suggests cholestatic jaundice, and the slow onset of disease, with initial symptoms of itching, and antimitochondrial antibody positivity, fits well with a diagnosis of PBC. Although smooth muscle antibodies are seen in autoimmune hepatitis, they are also a recognised finding in PBC.

Alcoholic cirrhosis
Alcoholic cirrhosis is incorrect. The very modest alcohol consumption and small elevation in γglutamyltransferase make a diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis less likely.

Autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis is incorrect. Although smooth muscle antibodies are present, the liver function test picture is much more suggestive of obstruction/cholestasis rather than hepatocellular dysfunction.

Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas is incorrect. Pancreatic carcinoma is associated with epigastric pain radiating to the back and progressive weight loss, neither of which are reported here.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is incorrect. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is more common in males than females, and 75% of cases are associated with inflammatory bowel disease.

stem: A 21-year-old male medical student who has been feeling non-specifically unwell for several days is noticed to have slightly icteric sclerae by his girlfriend and has liver function tests performed. The results of these are normal apart from a serum bilirubin concentration of 44 μmol/l (3–17). His urine does not contain bilirubin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gilbert’s syndrome
Gilbert’s may carry an autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, and the episode of jaundice here has been triggered by his non-specific illness and a potential reduction in calorie intake. No intervention is required, and jaundice resolves spontaneously, although phenobarbitone has been shown to accelerate metabolism of excess bilirubin.

Dubin–Johnson syndrome
Dubin–Johnson syndrome is incorrect. Dubin–Johnson syndrome is inherited with an autosomal recessive pattern, and is seen more frequently in patients of Jewish heritage. In most patients the jaundice is asymptomatic and remains at a low level, with no long-term sequelae. Bilirubin is conjugated and appears in the urine. Coproporphyrin excretion pattern can be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Hereditary spherocytosis
Hereditary spherocytosis is incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis is a chronic haemolytic disorder and presents with low-grade anaemia, intermittent jaundice and splenomegaly. Over the longer term it is also associated with increased risk of gallstones.

Infectious mononucleosis
Infectious mononucleosis is incorrect. Infectious mononucleosis is associated with a viral hepatitis, transaminases are elevated, and atypical lymphocytes are seen on the blood film. 10 A 71-year-old-man is given a health check by his doctor. He has no complaints, apart from pain in his hip, which he attributes to arthritis. He has blood taken for a panel of routine biochemical and haematological tests. The only abnormality is a serum alkaline phosphatase activity of 822 u/l. A routine hip and pelvis X-ray reveals arthritic changes around the right hip joint including acetabular protrusion and cortical thickening.

Rotor syndrome
Rotor syndrome is incorrect. Like Dubin–Johnson syndrome, rotor syndrome is associated with the appearance of conjugated bilirubin in the urine, and jaundice is usually apparent soon after birth.

stem: A 71-year-old-man is given a health check by his doctor. He has no complaints, apart from pain in his hip, which he attributes to arthritis. He has blood taken for a panel of routine biochemical and haematological tests. The only abnormality is a serum alkaline phosphatase activity of 822 u/l. A routine hip and pelvis X-ray reveals arthritic changes around the right hip joint including acetabular protrusion and cortical thickening. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this abnormality in his case?
explanation:
Paget’s disease
Elevated alkaline phosphatase activity is usually an indicator of bone or cholestatic hepatobiliary disease. The fact that other liver function tests are normal in this patient militates against (though does not exclude) the latter. An increase in alkaline phosphatase from bone reflects increased osteoclastic activity. The condition presents with excess osteoclastic activity followed by a compensatory increase in osteoblastic activity, leading to the formation of disorganized bone, which is less compact, mechanically weaker, highly vascular and more susceptible to fracture. Bisphosphonates are the intervention of choice.

Metastatic carcinoma
Metastatic carcinoma is incorrect. Given the patient has no other symptoms to suggest carcinomatosis, and only one joint is affected, Paget’s is the more likely underlying diagnosis.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. Osteoarthritis is not associated with biochemical abnormalities.

Osteomalacia
Osteomalacia is incorrect. Although osteomalacia is associated with elevated alkaline phosphatase, it is also associated with hypocalcaemia.

Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is incorrect. Osteoporosis is not associated with an elevated alkaline phosphatase unless there is a resultant fracture which has driven osteoblast activity.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic by her GP after she was found to have a serum calcium concentration of 3.12 mmol/l on routine blood testing. Which of the following clinical features, if present, would most direct you towards a specific cause?
explanation:
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
The presence of hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray in a patient with hypercalcaemia should raise a suspicion that the latter is due to sarcoid (in which the granulomas secrete calcitriol, 1,25dihydroxycholecalciferol). In this patient a history of shortness of breath or chronic cough should be elicited. Excess sun exposure and consumption of phosphate containing drinks can also drive up calcium levels.

Bone pain
Bone pain is incorrect. Bone pain can occur with hypercalcaemia secondary to malignancy or hyperparathyroidism and so is not a specific finding.

Polyuria
Polyuria is incorrect. Polyuria is a feature of severe hypercalcaemia, irrespective of the cause.

Short QT interval
Short QT interval is incorrect. A short QT interval is also a feature of hypercalcaemia, not a cause.

Ureteric colic
Ureteric colic is incorrect. Ureteric colic is particularly associated with primary hyperparathyroidism, but is not specific, as renal stones may be seen across a number of other causes of hypercalcaemia.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents with mild jaundice following a flu-like illness. Following review by a gastroenterologist, he has been told that a diagnosis of Gilbert’s syndrome is probable. Which of the following laboratory tests is most likely to confirm this diagnosis?
options: Absence of bilirubin in the urine
Elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (transaminase, AST) activity
explanation:
Absence of bilirubin in the urine
In Gilbert’s syndrome there is a defect in the UGT1A1 gene which leads to a defect in glucuronidation, and a consequent increase in unconjugated bilirubin. This leads to jaundice, but an absence of bilirubin in the urine.

Decreased serum haptoglobin concentration
Decreased serum haptoglobin concentration is incorrect. Decreased serum haptoglobin is more consistent with a diagnosis of haemolysis.

Elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (transaminase, AST) activity
Elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (transaminase, AST) activity is incorrect. Elevated serum transaminases are inconsistent with a diagnosis of Gilbert’s, because the sole defect is in glucuronidation.

Increased reticulocyte count
Increased reticulocyte count is incorrect. Increase in reticulocyte count is most likely to be seen in patients with haemolysis.

Increased urinary urobilinogen excretion
Increased urinary urobilinogen excretion is incorrect. Increased urinary urobilinogen excretion implies a degree of bilirubin conjugation which is not seen in patients with Gilbert’s syndrome.

stem: A 71-year-old man is referred by his GP to the Emergency Department, having presented with increasing nausea, shortness of breath and lethargy. The results of initial investigations include a serum Cr concentration of 654 μmol/l and a K + of 6.2 mmol/l. Which of the following best suggests a specific cause for his kidney disease?
explanation:
Bence Jones proteinuria
Excretion of immunoglobulin light chains suggests a diagnosis of myeloma. Myeloma can cause kidney disease through various mechanisms, including tubular obstruction by protein, particularly when there is coexistent dehydration /low urinary flow, and infiltration by amyloid.

Anaemia
Anaemia is incorrect. It is associated with chronic kidney disease irrespective of cause, due to decreased production of erythropoietin and bone marrow suppression.

Hyperuricaemia
Hyperuricaemia is incorrect. Although severe gout is associated with urate stones and consequent renal impairment, kidney disease per se is associated with reduced urate excretion, and as such is a non-specific finding.

Hypocalcaemia
Hypocalcaemia is incorrect. This occurs due to reduced renal hydroxylation of vitamin D, which is common across the various mechanisms of renal impairment.

Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic acidosis is incorrect. This is common across mechanisms of chronic kidney disease due to defects in bicarbonate reabsorption and acid secretion. Multiple Myeloma An overweight 32-year-old woman presents with a short history of painless jaundice. There is no previous history of illness and, apart from jaundice, the only signs of chronic liver disease are spider naevi on the upper body. Initial investigations reveal a Hb of 127 g/l, MCV 105 fl, serum bilirubin 162 μmol/l, AST 182 U/l, ALT 81 U/l, ALP 224 U/l and GGT 200 U/l.

stem: An overweight 32-year-old woman presents with a short history of painless jaundice. There is no previous history of illness and, apart from jaundice, the only signs of chronic liver disease are spider naevi on the upper body. Initial investigations reveal a Hb of 127 g/l, MCV 105 fl, serum bilirubin 162 μmol/l, AST 182 U/l, ALT 81 U/l, ALP 224 U/l and GGT 200 U/l. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
explanation:
Alcoholic liver disease
Jaundice with an elevation of both aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) suggests mixed hepatocellular damage and cholestatic liver disease, typical of acute alcoholic hepatitis on a background of chronic liver disease (and is not excluded by the lack of physical signs). The high γ-glutamyltransferase (GGT) and the fact that the AST: ALT ratio is greater than 2, lend further credence to alcohol as the underlying cause of her presentation. Macrocytosis is another feature typical of chronic excessive alcohol intake.

Autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis is incorrect. As jaundice in this condition is usually preceded by a period of severe tiredness, lethargy and itching. It is also associated with anti-smooth muscle antibody positivity and a picture more suggestive of hepatocellular dysfunction versus the partial obstructive picture seen here.

Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas is incorrect. This is associated with epigastric pain radiating to the back in the majority of cases, and a more obstructive picture on liver function testing.

Cholecystitis
Cholecystitis is incorrect. This is associated with right upper quadrant pain and obstructive jaundice, rather than the painless picture seen here.

Hepatitis A infection
Hepatitis A infection is incorrect. This is associated with a diarrhoeal illness and flu-like symptoms, and is followed some 1–2 weeks later by the onset of jaundice; it is also associated with hepatocellular dysfunction on liver function testing.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department, for the third time over the past 6 months, with hypertension and abdominal pain associated with significant distress. She has been diagnosed as suffering from acute intermittent porphyria. You are writing a management plan for colleagues in the event she presents on a further occasion for treatment. Which of the following is the most useful intervention?
explanation:
IV haem arginate
This suppresses hepatic haem synthesis that is responsible for the presentation with episodes of acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), leading to resolution of symptoms. A typical regimen involves giving 3–4 mg/kg/day over the course of 4 days.

Exchange transfusion
Exchange transfusion is incorrect. This does not have a role in the treatment of acute intermittent porphyria.

IV 5% dextrose
IV 5% dextrose is incorrect. This does not deliver an adequate carbohydrate load to impact on AIP, and care should be taken when giving glucose replacement to avoid worsening any associated hyponatraemia.

IV phenobarbitone
IV phenobarbitone is incorrect. This is a historical treatment for epilepsy and was used to resolve jaundice in Gilbert syndrome. Fits associated with AIP are treated with levetiracetam. Acute Intermittent Porphyria An elderly man with a history of prostatism presents with acute retention of urine. His serum Cr concentration is 520 μmol/l. Which of the following additional abnormal serum biochemistry test results is most suggestive of a chronic component to his kidney disease?

Oral cimetidine
Oral cimetidine is incorrect. This is an enzyme inhibitor that may reduce haem synthesis, although no randomised controlled trials (RCTs) support its use in AIP; haem arginate remains the first-choice intervention.

stem: An elderly man with a history of prostatism presents with acute retention of urine. His serum Cr concentration is 520 μmol/l. Which of the following additional abnormal serum biochemistry test results is most suggestive of a chronic component to his kidney disease?
explanation:
Hypocalcaemia
Its presence in kidney disease suggests that it is, at least in part, long-standing and owing to decreased renal synthesis of calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol). Vitamin D is supplemented in chronic kidney disease, but guidelines suggest that calcium and vitamin D supplementation is not begun until parathyroid hormone (PTH) has escaped twice the upper limit of the normal range.

Hyperkalaemia
Hyperkalaemia is incorrect. High potassium does not differentiate between acute and chronic kidney disease. Where a chronic rise is seen, it may be tolerated to a higher level versus acute potassium changes, although the management is the same, with IV calcium under cardiac monitoring being the initial step for severe hyperkalaemia.

Hyperuricaemia
Hyperuricaemia is incorrect. This can be seen in both acute and chronic kidney disease, due to failure of adequate urate excretion. It is of course a cause of acute and chronic kidney disease itself, due to urate nephropathy.

Hyponatraemia
Hyponatraemia is incorrect. Salt and water overload (leading to hyponatraemia because of decreased free water excretion) can be seen in both acute and chronic renal impairment.

Low serum bicarbonate concentration
Low serum bicarbonate concentration is incorrect. Due to defective H + excretion and defective bicarbonate retention, this is a feature of both acute and chronic kidney disease.

stem: A 68-year-old man undergoes a routine health check-up, which includes a physical examination and various laboratory investigations. An elevated BMI of 35 kg/m 2 is noted and he has abnormal results as follows: fasting blood glucose 8.0 mmol/l; corrected calcium 2.01 mmol/l; ALP activity 232 U/l (upper limit of reference range – 150); TSH 10.1 mU/l; Cr clearance (calculated) 70 ml/min (normal range: 85 – 125 µmol/min). Which one of the following parameters would be considered of least concern?
explanation:
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)
The GFR declines with ageing beyond 40 years, but serum concentrations of creatinine (Cr) and urea are usually not affected because of the concomitant decreases in muscle bulk and protein turnover, respectively.

Fasting blood glucose concentration
Fasting blood glucose concentration is incorrect. This is in the impaired fasting glucose range, putting this patient at increased risk of cardiovascular disease; he should therefore be encouraged to lose weight.

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity is incorrect. It is significantly elevated here, in conjunction with the hypocalcaemia, which is suggestive of osteomalacia.

Serum calcium
Serum calcium is incorrect. This patient is hypocalcaemic, coupled with the raised alkaline phosphatase, which is suggestive of a diagnosis of osteomalacia.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration is incorrect. It is significantly elevated, which may fit with subclinical hypothyroidism; measurement of free triiodothyronine (T3) and free thyroxine (T4) is therefore an essential next step.

stem: Which of the following fluids would be the most appropriate to replace the fluid being lost in a patient with a paralytic ileus draining 2 litres of fluid a day through a nasogastric tube?
options: 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium according to electrolytes
explanation:
0.9% sodium chloride with potassium according to electrolytes
To replace the fluid being lost in a patient with a paralytic ileus draining 2 litres of fluid a day through a nasogastric tube, it is essential to supply sufficient chloride ions to replace the chloride being lost in the gastric fluid (gastric juice is essentially dilute hydrochloric acid).

Compound sodium lactate (Hartmann’s solution)
Compound sodium lactate (Hartmann’s solution) is incorrect. This does not replace lost chloride ions, and the lactate it contains may be metabolised to bicarbonate, exacerbating alkalosis.

5% dextrose
A 70-year-old man with symptoms of prostatism has a serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level of 20 μg/l (normal value, < 4 μg/l). Which one of the following statements about the clinical importance of this result is the most likely?

0.18% sodium chloride with 4% dextrose
0.18% sodium chloride with 4% dextrose is incorrect. This does not contain adequate chloride replacement, therefore driving increased risk of metabolic alkalosis.

stem: A 70-year-old man with symptoms of prostatism has a serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level of 20 μg/l (normal value, < 4 μg/l). Which one of the following statements about the clinical importance of this result is the most likely?
options: It could be elevated because a digital rectal examination was performed 48 h before the blood
It could be elevated because of cancer elsewhere in the urinary tract
It is diagnostic of prostatic cancer
It is more likely to reflect prostatic cancer than benign prostatic hypertrophy
It is normal for a man of this age
explanation:
It is more likely to reflect prostatic cancer than benign prostatic hypertrophy
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is specific to the prostate, although not for cancer; however, the degree of elevation seen here, (5 times the upper limit of nor mal), is consistent with a cancer.

It could be elevated because a digital rectal examination was performed 48 h before the blood
It could be elevated because a digital rectal examination was performed 48 h before the blood sample was taken It could be elevated because a digital rectal examination was performed 48 h before the blood sample was Chat AI the Tutor taken is incorrect. Although digital rectal examination may be associated with small increases in with PSA, magnitude of increase seen here is inconsistent with examination alone.

It could be elevated because of cancer elsewhere in the urinary tract
It could be elevated because of cancer elsewhere in the urinary tract is incorrect. PSA is specific to the prostate gland.

It is diagnostic of prostatic cancer
It is diagnostic of prostatic cancer is incorrect. PSA may rarely be significantly elevated in other conditions apart from cancer, including prostatitis and benign prostatic hypertrophy, although not usually to this level.

It is normal for a man of this age

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of Type 1 diabetes comes to the nephrology clinic for review. His GP has attempted to start an ACE inhibitor, but was unable to. Although his creatinine stayed relatively stable, a significant increase in his potassium was seen; his BP is 142/82 mmHg. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal tubular acidosis type (RTA) IV
Acquired and usually seen in patients with mild kidney disease due to diabetes or tubulointerstitial renal disease. The underlying cause is thought to be resistance to the action of aldosterone.

Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is incorrect. This is associated with marked proteinuria, rather than hyperkalaemia.

Renal artery stenosis
Renal artery stenosis is incorrect. This is associated with an increase in creatinine as well as the increase in potassium seen here.

Renal tubular acidosis type (RTA) I
Renal tubular acidosis type (RTA) I is incorrect. Distal RTA is associated with hypokalaemia and renal calculi.

Renal tubular acidosis type (RTA) II
Renal tubular acidosis type (RTA) II is incorrect. Proximal renal tubular acidosis is associated with hypokalaemia, rather than the hyperkalaemia seen here.
