stem: A patient in the intensive care unit following liver transplant surgery has a metabolic alkalosis with a pH of 7.56 and an elevated serum bicarbonate. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Diuretic-induced volume depletion
Relative volume depletion is a feature of cirrhosis, due to hypoalbuminaemia driving low colloid osmotic pressure. This drives increased aldosterone, which is not adequately metabolised by an impaired liver. Furosemide use in the post-operative period further exacerbates alkalosis driven by hyperaldosteronism and could be responsible for the presentation here.

Acetazolamide use
Acetazolamide use is incorrect. This is used as a treatment for metabolic alkalosis rather than being a cause.

Hypermagnesaemia
Hypermagnesaemia is incorrect. Although elevated magnesium is a recognised association of metabolic alkalosis, it is not a cause.

Increased serum lactate
Increased serum lactate is incorrect. Lactate is associated with tissue hypoxia seen at the time of transplant, but is not a cause of alkalosis.

Increased urea metabolism
Increased urea metabolism is incorrect. Metabolic alkalosis is a driver for urea synthesis by the liver in cirrhosis, but urea synthesis is not a cause of increased pH.

stem: A 48-year-old woman is referred to the gastroenterology clinic for review. She has no significant past medical history of note, and drinks one bottle of wine per week. On examination her BP is 150/82 mmHg, and pulse is 67 bpm and regular; her BMI is 29 kg/m 2. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Blood testing has revealed elevated ALT, AST and GGT; the AST:ALT ratio is 1 : 1.2. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)
Given this patient’s BMI, modest alcohol consumption and AST:ALT ratio less than 2, NASH is the most likely diagnosis, as it is associated with raised transaminases and elevated GGT, as seen here. Elevated GGT is also markedly elevated in patients with biliary obstruction.

Alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH)
Alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH) with AI is Tutor Alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH) is incorrect. The AST:ALT ratio is less than 2 and alcohol Chat consumption modest, making NASH the more likely diagnosis.

Cholelithiasis
Cholelithiasis is incorrect. A rise in GGT would be expected, although a rise in alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and right upper quadrant pain would also be a feature.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. The menstrual cycle effectively being a natural form of venesection, presentation with liver disease in women due to haemochromatosis is very unusual.

Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease is incorrect. This usually presents in the second or third decade with abnormal liver function tests (LFTs), neuropsychiatric symptoms or unilateral motor dysfunction.

stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted by ambulance after falling into a river. He is pulled out by two friends but is thought to have inhaled a significant quantity of water. On examination in the Emergency Department his saturation is 90% on O 2 by mask. He is drowsy but conscious, with bradycardia, BP of 90/60 mmHg and a temperature of 34.8°C. Auscultation of his chest reveals wheeze and crackles consistent with fluid inhalation. Which one of the following is the most likely biochemical imbalance to be seen?
explanation:
Mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis
Inhalation of fluid leads to disordered gas exchange in patients with significant fluid aspiration, precipitating respiratory acidosis. Metabolic acid results from intravascular volume depletion, hypotension and consequent tissue hypoxia.

Low urea
Low urea is incorrect. Relative intravascular volume depletion results in either normal or elevated, rather than reduced, urea.

Compensated respiratory acidosis
Compensated respiratory acidosis is incorrect. Metabolic compensation for respiratory acidosis takes some 48– 72 hr, and given hypotension and bradycardia, reduced tissue perfusion drives metabolic acidosis.

Hypokalaemia
Hypokalaemia is incorrect. Normal or elevated potassium is seen in cases of significant inhalation of fluid. You are reviewing the clinical chemistry results of a 19-year-old South Asian woman who has moved to the UK. She eats a vegetarian diet and rarely ventures out of the house. On examination in the clinic her BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 70 bpm and regular, and her BMI is 22 kg/m 2. She complains of pain affecting both femurs and has evidence of proximal myopathy. Investigations:

Hyponatraemia
Hyponatraemia is incorrect. Normal or elevated sodium are seen in cases of large-volume fluid inhalation due to intravascular volume depletion.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteomalacia
Osteomalacia has a higher incidence in South Asians, particularly those who eat a vegetarian diet, and is associated with hypocalcaemia and an elevated alkaline phosphatase; a compensatory rise in parathyroid hormone (PTH) may also drive increased phosphate excretion. Vitamin D and calcium supplementation rapidly reverse the symptoms.

Hypoparathyroidism
Hypoparathyroidism is incorrect. The typical blood picture would be hypocalcaemia, but phosphate is elevated and alkaline phosphatase is in the normal range; PTH is, of course, low.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. In this case, with no significant past medical history, primary hyperparathyroidism would be expected; this is associated with hypercalcaemia.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism
Pseudohypoparathyroidism is incorrect. The blood picture is one of hypocalcaemia and elevated phosphate; however, there is PTH resistance, so levels of PTH are actually elevated.

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. Low calcium may be seen after thyroidectomy, but this is most often related to disruption of the parathyroids, and is transient.

stem: Which one of the following is the principal cause of the raised calcium, which is associated with sarcoidosis?
explanation:
Elevated 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol
Elevated 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D production by activated alveolar macrophages is increased in sarcoidosis, which results in increased efficiency of calcium absorption from the small intestine and consequent hypercalcaemia. It is also recognised that elevation of parathyroid hormone (PTH) may occur in conjunction with sarcoidosis, although this may just represent coexistent hyperparathyroidism by chance in many cases. Increase in dietary phosphate from Coca-Cola ® has been shown to increase the risk of renal stones and soft tissue calcification.

Elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH)
Elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) is incorrect. Sarcoidosis is associated with elevated vitamin D; it is therefore most likely to be associated with suppressed levels of PTH.

Elevated calcitonin
Elevated calcitonin is incorrect. Calcitonin levels may be elevated as a response to hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis but they are not the cause of the hypercalcaemia itself.

Elevated cholecalciferol
Elevated cholecalciferol is incorrect. It is the hydroxylated form of vitamin D that is increased in patients with sarcoidosis.

Elevated calcitroic acid
Elevated calcitroic acid is incorrect. Although this is the metabolite of hydroxylated vitamin D, it is not the principal cause of hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis.

stem: A 30-year-old man is referred to the rheumatology clinic complaining of pain in his hips and back on walking. He has also begun to develop a dusky pigmentation discoloration, affecting his ears in particular, and has some calcification of the pinnae on examination. There is a family history of alkaptonuria. Which step in metabolism is altered in a patient with alkaptonuria?
explanation:
Amino acid metabolism
Alkaptonuria occurs because of a homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency that leads to a defect in tyrosine metabolism and accumulation of homogentisic acid. There is increased incidence of the disease in individuals who are HLA-DR7-positive. Symptoms occur owing to homogentisic acid accumulation and calcification. Dietary reduction of tyrosine and phenylalanine may reduce homogentisic acid accumulation and symptoms if instituted early.

Purine metabolism
Purine metabolism is incorrect. Excess purine synthesis or reduced purine breakdown is responsible for the development of gout.

Pyrimidine metabolism
Pyrimidine metabolism is incorrect. Such disorders can lead to megaloblastic anaemia, renal disorders and congenital cardiovascular disease; an example is hereditary orotic aciduria.

Glycoprotein metabolism
Glycoprotein metabolism is incorrect. Disorders in glycoprotein and glycolipid metabolism usually result from defects in lysosomal function; an example is galactosialidosis.

Carbohydrate metabolism
Carbohydrate metabolism is incorrect. Diabetes is the prime example of a disorder of carbohydrate metabolism.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with excess hair and amenorrhoea. She is normotensive. Her prolactin levels are normal but she has a raised 17α-hydroxyprogesterone level and testosterone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Partial 21-hydroxylase deficiency
This patient has congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). The most common type of CAH is 21-hydroxylase deficiency (autosomal-recessive) affecting around 1 in 10,000 White ethnicity; as a result, cortisol levels are low and trigger ACTH release and adrenal hyperplasia. 21-hydroxylase is responsible for metabolizing 17hydroxyprogesterone and progesterone itself, so absence or partial functioning of the enzyme leads to accumulation of 17-hydroxyprogesterone and other hormones leading to virilisation.

Complete 11β-hydroxylase deficiency
Complete 11β-hydroxylase deficiency is incorrect. 11-beta hydroxylase deficiency drives accumulation of corticosteroids one step further along the synthesis pathway, so 11-deoxycortisol and deoxycorticosterone levels are elevated.

Complete 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Complete 21-hydroxylase deficiency is incorrect. Complete 21-hydroxylase deficiency normally presents with symptoms of salt wasting in childhood, and more marked virilisation in girls. Patients with complete 21hydroxylase deficiency may require salt supplementation.

Partial 11β-hydroxylase deficiency
Partial 11β-hydroxylase deficiency is incorrect. The fact 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels are elevated here counts against 11beta hydroxylase deficiency as the underlying diagnosis.

17-hydroxylase deficiency
17-hydroxylase deficiency is incorrect. 17-hydroxylase deficiency presents with delayed puberty and symptoms of mineralocorticoid excess. You are investigating the effects of a new agent in the treatment of elevated LDL cholesterol.

stem: You are investigating the effects of a new agent in the treatment of elevated LDL cholesterol. Which of the following is a key feature of low-density lipoproteins (LDL)?
options: Levels are increased by PCSK9 inhibition
Their concentration is highly correlated with dietary cholesterol content
They are involved in reverse cholesterol transport
They are synthesised de novo in the liver
explanation:
They contain apolipoprotein B-100
Each particle of LDL contains one molecule of apolipoprotein B-100, the ligand for the LDL receptor.

Levels are increased by PCSK9 inhibition
Levels are increased by PCSK9 inhibition is incorrect. PCSK9 drives LDL receptor degradation and when liver LDL receptor levels fall, LDL levels rise. Inhibition of PCSK9 (a drug target), in contrast results in a fall in LDL.

Their concentration is highly correlated with dietary cholesterol content
Their concentration is highly correlated with dietary cholesterol content is incorrect. The concentration of LDLs is determined mainly by the rates of hepatic synthesis and peripheral clearance.Dietary saturated fat intake correlates more strongly than dietary cholesterol intake with LDL-cholesterol concentration.

They are involved in reverse cholesterol transport
They are involved in reverse cholesterol transport is incorrect. HDL cholesterol is involved in reverse cholesterol transport. A 72 year old woman presents to the Emergency department with gradually worsening nausea, vomiting and drowsiness. According to relatives she has suffered from a chronic cough for some time, and has gradually lost weight. She continues to smoke 10 cigarettes per day. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 148/82, pulse is 72 and regular. Auscultation of the chest reveals crackles and quiet wheeze consistent with COPD. Abdomen is soft and non-tender with a BMI of 22. Bloods taken in the emergency department reveal a creatinine of 175 micromol/l (60-110), and a calcium of 3.4 mmol/l, (2.1-2.65). Which of the following malignancies would you consider as the most likely underlying cause?

They are synthesised de novo in the liver
They are synthesised de novo in the liver is incorrect. LDLs are formed from VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein) and IDL (intermediate-density lipoprotein) by successive removal of triglyceride and modification in the circulation.

stem: A 72 year old woman presents to the Emergency department with gradually worsening nausea, vomiting and drowsiness. According to relatives she has suffered from a chronic cough for some time, and has gradually lost weight. She continues to smoke 10 cigarettes per day. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 148/82, pulse is 72 and regular. Auscultation of the chest reveals crackles and quiet wheeze consistent with COPD. Abdomen is soft and non-tender with a BMI of 22. Bloods taken in the emergency department reveal a creatinine of 175 micromol/l (60-110), and a calcium of 3.4 mmol/l, (2.1-2.65). Which of the following malignancies would you consider as the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Squamous-cell carcinoma of the bronchus
Given the history of smoking and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), underlying bronchial carcinoma should be considered as the most likely cause of hypercalcaemia. Squamous cell carcinomas are more likely to produce PTHrp, renal, bladder, breast and ovarian cancers are other solid tumours known to produce the hormone.

Bronchial carcinoid
Bronchial carcinoid is incorrect. Bronchial carcinoid is more likely to present at a younger age with obstructive symptoms leading to lobar pneumonia, or pulmonary haemorrhage due to the vascular nature of the tumour, and isn’t linked to smoking.

Lymphoma
Lymphoma is incorrect. The chest symptoms and smoking history count more towards an underlying bronchial carcinoma versus a lymphoma. Lymphomas can be associated with hypercalcaemia, this may be due to unregulated extrarenal production of calcitriol.

Multiple myeloma
Multiple myeloma is incorrect. Multiple myeloma may be responsible for hypercalcaemia, although this is most likely to be seen in patients with advanced disease, due to osteoclast activity.

Small-cell carcinoma of the bronchus
Small-cell carcinoma of the bronchus is incorrect. Small cell carcinoma of the bronchus is less likely versus squamous cell carcinoma to lead to hypercalcaemia. stem: A 22 year old man presents to the endocrine clinic with recurrent balanitis and is found to have a fasting plasma glucose of 8.0 mmol/l. He has a history in the family of type 2 diabetes. His weight has been stable over the past few months. On examination his BP is 110/70, pulse is 70 bpm and regular. His BMI is 23. Anti-GAD antibodies are weakly positive. Which of the following features in his history and examination makes us more likely to think of underlying type 2 diabetes rather than type 1 diabetes?
explanation:
Lack of recent weight loss
Although not invariably, type 1 diabetes is likely to be associated with symptoms of insulinopaenia at presentation, these include polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss. The lack of weight loss hints at an alternative diagnosis, and given the strong family history of type 2 diabetes, MODY is a possibility.

Fasting plasma glucose 8.0
Fasting plasma glucose 8.0 is incorrect. The fasting plasma glucose of 8.0 is in the diabetic range, and may indicate the early stages of type 1 diabetes or indeed type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Onset age 22
Onset age 22 is incorrect. Although type 2 diabetes was historically associated with older age at onset, it’s now diagnosed in children as young as 11 years of age.

Positive anti-GAD antibodies
Positive anti-GAD antibodies is incorrect. The GAD antibody titre is only weakly positive, hence it’s not a strong pointer to either type 1 or type 2 diabetes.

Recurrent balanitis
Recurrent balanitis is incorrect. Recurrent balanitis is merely associated with increased glucose levels.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents to the clinic some 2 years after diagnosis with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her weight is 86 kg, body mass index 36 kg/m 2. Current medication is oral metformin 1g twice per day. Other past history of note includes a previous inferior myocardial infarction some 5 years earlier. On examination her BP is 142/82, pulse is 72 and regular. Her chest is clear, there is mild pitting oedema of both ankles which may be related to use of amlodipine. A recent HbA1c is 71 mmol/mol, and her creatinine is 95 micromol/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Empagliflozin
Empagliflozin is an SGLT-2 inhibitor, which leads to renal excretion of glucose and has positive effects on HbA1c and is associated with minor, (2-3% loss in weight on average), over a 6 month period. It also has a positive impact on cardiovascular mortality as evidenced by the EMPA-REG study. Given this patient’s positive history with respect to ischaemic heart disease, and significant obesity, it is therefore the most appropriate option.

Acarbose
Acarbose is incorrect. Although acarbose is an option for controlling blood glucose, its effects are modest in lowering HbA1c, and it is often poorly tolerated in combination with metformin due to abdominal pain, flatulence and diarrhea.

Glipizide
Glipizide is incorrect. In this situation even a short acting sulphonylurea is likely to promote weight gain and may be associated with both fluid retention and hypoglycaemia.

Liraglutide
Liraglutide is incorrect. A GLP-1 agonist is a potential option for this patient because it promotes both glucose control and weight loss, but is most likely to be used in addition to dual oral therapy.

Sitagliptin
Sitagliptin is incorrect. Sitagliptin is a DPPIV inhibitor. Although it has potential advantages in this patient, (it is weight neutral and does not cause hypoglycaemia), an SGLT-2 inhibitor is preferred because of modest positive effects with respect to weight control. stem: Blood buffers are essential for maintaining the body’s acid-base balance. Which of the following is a blood buffer?
explanation:
Haemoglobin
Haemoglobin is a protein and has imidazole side chains which can buffer H + ions. Along with bicarbonate, it is one of the most important buffering agents in plasma. Deoxyhaemoglobin is a much more effective buffer than oxyhaemoglobin which accounts for some proportion of the Haldane effect (the effect of oxygen on haemoglobin, reducing its ability to transport carbon dioxide).

Carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide is incorrect. Carbon dioxide is absorbed into the bloodstream and with water will form carbonic acid. However, the presence of bicarbonate in the blood acts as a buffer such that there is minimal change in blood pH with the absorption of carbon dioxide.

Potassium
Potassium is incorrect. A buffer must be able to accept H + ions; potassium is a cation and therefore cannot accept H + ions.

Sodium
Sodium is incorrect. A buffer must be able to accept H + ions; sodium is a cation and therefore cannot accept H + ions.

Urea
Urea is incorrect. Urea is not a base, and does not contain any side groups that can accept H + ions, therefore it cannot act as a buffer. Buffers are substances or solutions that accept a proton or hydroxyl group with very little change in overall pH. Blood buffers include bicarbonate, haemoglobin and protein. Technically phosphate is also a serum buffer but so little of it is present in the plasma that it has no significant contribution to the body’s acid-base balance mechanisms. Haemoglobin has imidazole side chains which can accept hydrogen ions. Haemoglobin is a much more effective buffer in its deoxygenated form, which contributes to the Haldane effect. This is where carbon dioxide is offloaded more easily at the lungs (when haemoglobin is oxygenated) but is easily picked up and transported from the tissues (when haemoglobin has been deoxygenated).

stem: He begins a total parenteral nutrition (TPN) regimen, but unfortunately, suffers decreased consciousness and a short tonic–clonic seizure. In this case, deficiency of which one of the following is the most likely cause of the change in consciousness?
explanation:
Phosphate
Phosphate is the correct answer. Any patient with a drastically reduced nutrient intake for consecutive days or has had a critical illess/major surgery is at risk of developing refeeding syndrome when feeding is recommenced, potentially leading to neurologic, pulmonary, cardiac, neuromuscular, and hematologic complications. The hallmark biochemical feature of re-feeding syndrome is hypophosphataemia, which leads to cardiac, respiratory and neuromuscular failure. Other central nervous system manifestations include metabolic encephalopathy as a result of ATP depletion, which may include altermed mental status, parastheisa, seizures and coma. However, the syndrome is complex and may also feature abnormal sodium and fluid balance; changes in glucose, protein and fat metabolism; thiamine deficiency; hypokalaemia; and hypomagnesaemia. In this case, thiamine should be replaced before starting feeding, and phosphate replacement added to the bags.

Niacin
Niacin is incorrect. Deficiency of niacin leads to pellagra, a multi-system condition that commonly causes diarrhoea, dermatitis and dementia.

Sodium
Sodium is incorrect. Symptoms and signs of hyponatremia are non-specific and may include the following: nausea and vomiting, confusion, lethargy, fatigue and decreased consciousness. Symptom severity depends on the speed of the drop in blood sodium. A gradual drop, even to very low levels, may be tolerated well if it occurs over several days or weeks. Replacement of sodium should occur gradually in order to avoid the risk of developing central pointe myelinolysis.

Glucose
Although hypoglycaemia is common in patients with alcoholism, carbohydrate forms a major component of refeeding solution, meaning that hypoglycaemia is very unlikely in this situation.

Potassium
Potassium is incorrect. Mild hypokalaemia is often asymptomatic but may lead to the development of arrhythmias. Severe hypokalaemia may cause muscles weakness, cramps, respiratory depression and paralysis.

stem: A 72-year-old man has pain in his left hip which has progressively worsened over the past six months, such that his movement is now severely limited. Examination reveals severe limitation of flexion and external rotation of the left hip. A hip X-ray shows gross deformity of the joint with loss of joint space and extensive new bone formation. You suspect Paget’s disease. Which of the following is most likely to be elevated?
explanation:
Alkaline phosphatase
Alkaline phosphatase is a marker of osteoblast activity. It correlates well with symptoms of Paget’s disease and responds to treatment with bisphosphonates. If there is debate about whether the alkaline phosphatase is bony in origin or from the liver, then measurement of the bone-specific enzyme may be useful. Symptom relief is the goal of intervention with bisphosphonates rather than aiming to normalise alkaline phosphatase.

Calcium
Calcium is normal in patients with Paget’s disease and has no value as a measure of disease activity. Small elevations in calcium may be seen in patients with Paget’s who spend a prolonged period of time bedbound.

Magnesium
Low serum magnesium concentrations are associated with highly active Paget's disease; they do not arise from increased urinary loss nor from a lowered net absorption of magnesium, but probably from increased uptake by bone. Increased levels are not therefore a feature in patients with Paget’s disease symptoms.

Phosphate
Phosphate accumulation is seen in patients with chronic renal impairment and in patients with hypoparathyroidism. It is not a feature of Paget’s disease. Low-phosphate diet and use of phosphate binders are integral to the management of patients with more advanced chronic kidney disease.

Vitamin D
Elevated vitamin D is seen in patients with hypercalcaemia related to active sarcoidosis, where production of 1,25-OH vitamin D is increased. Elevated vitamin D does not have a role in the pathogenesis of Paget’s disease.

stem: Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the initial treatment of choice?
explanation:
IV infusion of hypertonic saline
Acute (< 48 hours) symptomatic hyponatraemia necessitates prompt correction, as the rapid rate of change in serum Na + levels does not allow for equilibration of Na + between the intravascular and extravascular spaces. This can be particularly problematic in the brain. When the serum Na + level falls sharply, the interstitium within the CNS becomes relatively hypertonic, leading to movement of water from the serum. Given the volumetric constraints of the skull, this cerebral oedema can quickly lead to coma, seizures, brainstem herniation and death. Prompt administration of hypertonic saline (3%) is therefore indicated, typically as an infusion in 100-ml increments over ten minutes until symptoms . The maximum daily rate of serum Na+ correction must also be controlled because there is a risk of central pontine myelinolysis with rapid overcorrection. Guidelines can vary, but they generally advise an increase of serum Na + of 8–12 mmol in the first day for severe cases, followed by 4–6 mmol/day. Clinical manifestations of central pontine myelinolysis may include dysarthria, dysphagia, para-/quadriparesis, seizures, confusion, coma and, rarely, locked-in syndrome.

IV infusion of isotonic saline
IV infusion of isotonic saline will not significantly raise the serum Na + level in a patient who is euvolaemic with hyponatraemia. Fluid restriction is therefore preferred.

Oral demeclocycline
Oral demeclocycline promotes free water loss, leading to an increase in the serum Na + level and is a possible intervention in the event that fluid retention alone fails to correct the problem.

Oral furosemide
Furosemide promotes both Na + and water loss. As such, it is not appropriate as monotherapy for syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) and, indeed in this situation, may promote pre-kidney disease.

Restriction of water intake
Restriction of water intake is the initial treatment of choice for hyponatraemic patients with SIADH who are not at imminent risk of seizures or coma and who have a serum Na + level of 130 mEq/l or above. This precipitates a gradual rise in the serum Na + level, not greater than the recommended maximum of 8–10 mmol/day.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with known renal disease presents to the Emergency Department. Her admission biochemistry profile shows a serum K + concentration of 6.2 mmol/l; her ECG is abnormal. Which ECG abnormality is most likely to have occurred earliest as her hyperkalaemia developed?
explanation:
Tall, tented T waves
The development of tall tented T waves is typically seen early in the time course of hyperkalaemia.

Prolonged PR interval
Prolonged PR interval is incorrect. This is typically seen where potassium (K +) is greater than 6.5 mmol/l, and represents progressive paralysis of the atria.

Prominent U waves
Prominent U waves is incorrect. These are a feature of hypo- rather than hyperkalaemia, which is seen here.

Reduced P wave amplitude
Reduced P wave amplitude is incorrect. Like PR prolongation, is seen when potassium (K +) is greater than 6.5 mmol/l and at K+ levels greater than 7.5 mmol/l the P wave disappears.

Sine wave pattern
Sine wave pattern is incorrect. This is seen on ECG as a preterminal change, and is associated with potassium (K +) levels greater than 7.0 mmol/l.

stem: A young couple in their twenties presents to the Genetics Clinic to discuss the risk of future children they may have suffering from liver failure. Apparently, a niece died in very early childhood, suffering from progressive jaundice in infancy. No other family members have been affected, and the family remember there was a marked rise in unconjugated bilirubin in the child. Which of the following fits best with the underlying inherited condition?
explanation:
Autosomally inherited, severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Crigler–Najjar is a rare syndrome that can be either autosomal-recessive (type 1) or autosomal-recessive with pseudodominance (type 2). Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia results from an absence (type 1) or decrease (type 2) of glucuronyl transferase. As, in effect, it is a prehepatic problem, liver histology is normal and only those with the type-2 disease can survive to adulthood. Liver transplantation is the only effective intervention.

Autosomally-dominant, severe conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Autosomal-dominant, severe conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is incorrect. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is seen in both Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndrome, Dubin-Johnson carries an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

Autosomal-recessive, mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Autosomal-recessive, mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is incorrect. Gilbert’s syndrome is an example of an autosomal recessive condition associated with mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

X-linked, severe conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
X-linked, severe conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is incorrect. X-linked severe conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is not well described, and the fact that a niece was affected, makes an X-linked condition less likely.

X-linked, severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
X-linked, severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is incorrect. G6PD deficiency is X-linked and results in neonatal jaundice.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with a family history of early death due to ischaemic heart disease comes to the clinic for review. She is worried about making sure her blood pressure and lipids are well controlled. Her BP is measured at 142/72 mmHg, and fasting cholesterol is measured at 8.4 mmol/l, with an LDL of 5.7 mmol/l; TSH is 2.5 mU/l (NR 0.4–5). Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
LDL receptor mutation
Mutations in the LDL-receptor gene lead to the development of familial hypercholesterolaemia. Homozygosity leads to higher levels of cholesterol, with total cholesterol levels of 15 mmol/l not unusual in this situation. Treatment in this woman’s case is with high-dose statin therapy, +/- addition of other lipid-lowering agents such as evolocumab or ezetimibe.

Chylomicron retention
Chylomicron retention is incorrect. This is associated with malabsorption of fats, diarrhoea and neurological disorders.

HDL receptor mutation
High-density lipoprotein (HDL)-receptor mutation is incorrect. Mutations in the HDL scavenger receptor lead to premature cardiovascular disease, but not a large rise in LDL cholesterol.

Increased secretion of VLDL
Increased secretion of very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) is incorrect. This is associated with a rise in triglycerides.

Lipoprotein lipase deficiency
Familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency is incorrect. This is very rare and results in marked elevation of triglycerides, eruptive xanthomata and recurrent pancreatitis.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes reports at her regular clinic review that she has been experiencing frequent episodes of hypoglycaemia during the previous 6 months, despite reducing her overall dose of insulin by almost 50%. Her HbA1c in the clinic is 36 mmol/mol having been 45 mmol/mol a year previously. She says that her periods are becoming scanty and irregular and wonders if she is having an early menopause. Her gonadotrophin concentrations are low. What is the most likely cause of the reduction in her insulin requirement?
explanation:
Hypopituitarism
Both decreased secretion of cortisol and growth hormone can drive a reduction in insulin requirements because these are counter-regulatory hormones with respect to insulin action. The progressively more scanty and irregular periods also fit loss of gonadotrophin release, suggesting hypopituitarism because of deficiency of multiple pituitary hormones.

Addison’s disease
Addison’s disease is incorrect. The features here including sex hormone dysfunction are more supportive of hypopituitarism rather than isolated cortisol deficiency.

Increased exercise
Increased exercise is incorrect. Increased exercise would not drive as great a reduction in insulin dose as that seen here, making a reduction in counter-regulatory hormones the more likely driver for hypoglycaemia.

Spontaneous regression of diabetes
Spontaneous regression of diabetes is incorrect. Although patients with type 1 diabetes may enter a honeymoon period soon after diagnosis, spontaneous regression of diabetes is not seen in established disease.

Weight loss
Weight loss is incorrect. Marked weight loss is not reported by the patient here, implying that it cannot be the driver for the reduction in insulin dose.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with global weakness, lethargy and numbness of her extremities, which has worsened over the past 6 weeks; she admits to intermittent diarrhoea. On examination in the Emergency Department, she is markedly underweight with a body mass index (BMI) of only 18 kg/m 2. Her blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg and blood testing reveals hypokalaemia, raised chloride levels, low serum bicarbonate and a pH of 7.31. Which of the following diagnoses seems most likely in this case?
explanation:
Laxative abuse
This patient has a hypokalaemic, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. The most likely cause is gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonate and potassium due to chronic severe laxative abuse. While mild laxative abuse results in alkalosis, more severe loss of bicarbonate eventually leads to acidosis. Diagnosis would be supported by urine testing for metabolites of commonly used laxative agents.

Bartter syndrome
Bartter syndrome is incorrect. This is associated with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis due to defective reabsorption of chloride in the thick ascending loop of Henle.

Liddle syndrome
Liddle syndrome is incorrect. This is associated with increased activity of the epithelial sodium channel, which promotes salt and water retention, driving hypokalaemia and hypertension.

Gitelman syndrome
Gitelman syndrome is incorrect. This, like Bartter’s, is due to defective chloride reabsorption and is associated with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.

Diuretic abuse
Diuretic abuse is incorrect. Although diuretic abuse would lead to marked potassium loss, it is associated with alkalosis rather than acidosis.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is asked to attend the endocrine clinic having had a routine blood test at the GP surgery which revealed hypercalcaemia with a calcium of 2.88 mmol/l. She has had mild asthma for the past 40 years, takes a salbutamol inhaler, and uses amlodipine for control of blood pressure. Physical examination is unremarkable with a blood pressure of 122/82, pulse is 65 and regular. Heart sounds are normal, her chest is clear. Her BMI is 23. Renal function is normal with a creatinine of 82. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hypercalcaemia?
explanation:
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Two of the commonest causes of hypercalcaemia in the western world are primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy. In primary hyperparathyroidism there is excess production of parathyroid hormone (PTH); although usually from a benign adenoma, this sometimes results from hyperplasia of the parathyroid glands and, in very rare cases, a carcinoma. The unremarkable findings on examination, coupled with absence of other significant pathology, make primary hyperparathyroidism the most likely answer.

Milk–alkali syndrome
Milk–alkali syndrome is incorrect. The milk–alkali syndrome can occur in patients who suffer from dyspepsia and drink milk and alkali-containing antacids, which may reduce the renal excretion of calcium. The condition is rarely seen now because of use of proton pump inhibitors.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. Sarcoidosis leading to hypercalcaemia is likely to be associated with respiratory symptoms, including a chronic cough.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Given renal function is normal, secondary hyperparathyroidism is unlikely as the cause for her hypercalcaemia.

Squamous-cell carcinoma
Squamous-cell carcinoma is incorrect. Given the absence of a smoking history and benign findings on examination, an underlying bronchial carcinoma as the cause of hyperclacaemia is unlikely.

stem: Which one of the following enzymes is specifically raised in the serum of patients with Gaucher’s disease?
explanation:
Acid phosphatase
Minor elevations of liver enzymes are common in Gaucher’s disease, but it is acid phosphatase and angiotensinconverting enzyme that are most commonly raised in the serum. Gaucher's disease is the most common lysosomal storage disease; it is caused by deficient activity of acid beta-glucosidase, leading to the deposition of glucocerebroside in cells of the macrophage–monocyte system. It is classified into three subtypes, nonneuropathic, acute neuropathic and chronic neuropathic. Recombinant glucosidase and glucosylceramide inhibitors (e.g. miglustat) are the mainstay of therapy.

Alanine transaminase (ALT)
Alanine transaminase (ALT) is incorrect. This is a marker of hepatocellular injury that may be elevated due any underlying liver disease, and is not specific for Gaucher’s.

Aspartate transaminase (AST)
Aspartate transaminase (AST) is incorrect. Similar to ALT, AST is a marker of parenchymal liver injury. However, unlike ALT, AST is much less specific to the liver and may also be elevated due to other conditions such as myocardial infarction.

Gamma-GT (GGT)
Gamma-GT (GGT) is incorrect. GGT is another non-specific marker predominantly used in the diagnosis of liver disease. In particular, it is helpful in diagnosing diseases of the biliary tree and is also elevated in conjunction with excess alcohol consumption.

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is incorrect. ALP is used as a marker of liver disease but is also present in several other tissues throughout the entire body, such as the liver, bile duct, kidneys, bones and placenta. stem: A 25-year-old woman is referred to the General Medical Clinic after being admitted to the Emergency Department with confusion and agitation, abdominal pain and hypertension. An astute junior in the department sent a urine sample for porphyrins, which was found to be positive. Which one of the following features would most suggest lead poisoning rather than acute intermittent porphyria as a cause of her presentation?
explanation:
Anaemia
Anaemia occurs only in lead poisoning and is due to inhibition of ferrochelatase (the activity of this enzyme is normal in acute intermittent porphyria), a decrease in red cell lifespan, and inhibition of pyrimidine 5'nucleotidase leading to the accumulation of pyrimidine nucleotides in red cells, which in turn reduces the stability of the cell membrane (and is seen on a blood film as basophilic stippling).

Abdominal pain
Abdominal pain with AIand Tutoris Abdominal pain. Abdominal pain is a feature of both lead poisoining and acute intermittent Chat porphyria, therefore not a differentiator here.

Foot drop
Foot drop is incorrect. Motor neuropathy including foot drop is a feature of both diagnoses.

Hypertension
Hypertension is incorrect. Hypertension is a feature of acute porphyrias, but is not normally seen in patients with lead poisoning.

Seizures
Seizures is incorrect. Although encephalopathy with seizures is more common in children with lead poisoning, it is still seen in adults with lead poisoning and in those with acute porphyrias. stem: A 54-year-old woman has undergone some blood tests as part of an employment health screen. She reports she is in good health and, being very health conscious, takes regular vitamin and mineral supplements. She is taking bendrofluazide 2.5 mg for hypertension and her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg. The only abnormalities are a serum calcium concentration of 2.94 mmol/l and a phosphate level just under the lower end of the normal range. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Primary hyperparathyroidism
The fact that this individual is asymptomatic, and the elevated calcium with a phosphate at the lower end of the normal range, make primary hyperparathyroidism the most likely diagnosis.

Diuretic treatment
Diuretic treatment with Diuretic treatment is incorrect. Although thiazides can cause hypercalcaemia and increased Chat urinary phosphate excretion, the effect is usually mild and unlikely to cause such a high calcium level.

High dietary calcium intake
High dietary calcium intake is incorrect. High dietary calcium intake doesn’t usually lead to systemic hypercalcaemia, as it’s under hormonal control via hydroxylated vitamin D.

High dietary vitamin D intake
High dietary cholecalciferol intake is incorrect. Hypercalcaemia due to increased cholecalciferol intake alone is rare, as quite large quantities of vitamin D are required to cause overdose. It’s more likely to be seen against a background of other conditions which pre-dispose to hypercalcaemia such as sarcoidosis.

Occult malignancy
Occult malignancy is incorrect. We’re not given any history of symptoms suggestive of underlying malignancy, and she only presented to medical services because of an insurance medical.

stem: In an adult patient with cirrhosis, which of the following findings is the most reliable diagnostic indicator that hereditary haemochromatosis is the cause of his underlying condition?
explanation:
Liver biopsy
In hereditary haemochromatosis (HH), the excess iron is primarily found in parenchymal cells, whereas with secondary iron overload, accumulation tends to be in Kupffer cells. Liver biopsy can demonstrate this, allows assessment of liver damage and is of prognostic value.

Serum ferritin concentration
Serum ferritin concentration is incorrect. Serum ferritin concentration is almost always markedly elevated in haemochromatosis, but elevations can occur in any inflammatory condition (including other Chat liver with diseases) as ferritin is an acute phase protein.

Serum iron concentration
Serum iron concentration is incorrect. Serum iron concentration is normal in approximately 25% of patients with HH and can be elevated in healthy individuals or people with secondary iron overload.

Serum total iron-binding capacity
Serum total iron-binding capacity is incorrect. Serum total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) reflects the transferrin concentration, which is usually normal in haemochromatosis, although TIBC can also be reduced.

Transferrin saturation
Transferrin saturation is incorrect. Transferrin saturation is typically high in HH, although it can also be increased in other iron-overload conditions and in liver disease. Molecular genetic analysis is also a useful option. Homozygosity for the C282Y mutation, or compound heterozygosity for C282Y and H63D, can identify asymptomatic individuals at risk of developing clinical haemochromatosis.

stem: A 45-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department unconscious and hyperventilating. His breath smells of alcohol. He owns a garage which apparently has money problems, and according to colleagues who accompany him to the Emergency Department, he has been drinking at work. Which of the following findings would most suggest that ethylene glycol had been consumed?
explanation:
Serum calcium concentration (corrected) 1.62 mmol/l
The principle end product of metabolism of ethylene glycol that causes significant toxicity is oxalic acid. This then combines with calcium to form insoluble calcium oxalate and drives presentation with acidosis and kidney disease. The treatment for ethylene glycol overdose is an inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase such as ethanol itself or fomepizole.

Blood glucose concentration of 12 mmol/l
Blood glucose concentration of 12 mmol/l is incorrect. A blood glucose level of 12 mmol/l is a very non-specific finding and cannot be attributed to a particular cause of poisoning.

Ketonuria
Ketonuria with Ketonuria is incorrect. Ketosis is seen in diabetic ketoacidosis, alcoholic ketoacidosis and in Chat patients with prolonged fasting; it is therefore not specific to ethylene glycol consumption.

Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic acidosis is incorrect. Although metabolic acidosis is associated with ethylene glycol poisoing, it may be associated with other agents in overdose/poisoning such as metformin, methanol and salicylate.

Serum sodium concentration 131 mmol/l
Serum sodium concentration 131 mmol/l is incorrect. Hyponatraemia is associated with a number of potential diagnoses, including ethanol abuse.

stem: You are asked to review a 71-year-old patient who has received excess blood transfusions and saline fluid replacement after a bleed following left total hip replacement. You estimate that approximately a 20% increase in his blood volume has occurred. What physiological process is most likely to correct this abnormality?
options: Increased activity of renal sympathetic nerves
explanation:
Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) release
ANP is a 28 amino acid peptide which is released in response to atrial stretch, likely to be associated with the 20% increase in blood volume. ANP dilates the afferent glomerular arteriole, constricts the efferent glomerular arteriole, and drives an increase in glomerular filtration rate (GFR). This then leads to an increase in salt and water excretion.

Aldosterone release Tutor Aldosterone release is incorrect. Aldosterone release drives salt and water retention, not required in AI this situation.

Increased activity of renal sympathetic nerves
Increased activity of renal sympathetic nerves is incorrect. Renal sympathetic nerve activity drives an increase in blood pressure rather than a reduction, and potentially promotes further salt and water retention.

Reduced activity of carotid baroreceptors
Reduced activity of carotid baroreceptors is incorrect. The greater impact on sodium and water excretion comes from ANP release related to atrial stretch.

Venous dilatation
Venous dilatation is incorrect. Venous dilatation may occur to modulate blood pressure, but does not reduce circulating blood volume. stem: You are reviewing blood results on a 49-year-old man who has presented with cirrhosis related to excess alcohol consumption. You note that he has metabolic alkalosis. Which of the following is the likely primary pathological mechanism?
options: Reduced bicarbonate secretion from the pancreas
Reduced lactate formation in skeletal muscle
explanation:
Relative intravascular volume depletion
In cirrhosis, the low albumin associated with severe disease drives relative intravascular volume depletion. Aldosterone release is increased as a result, and steroid hormone metabolism is reduced by liver impairment. Both of these factors drive presentation with metabolic alkalosis. Additionally, albumin behaves as a weak acid and a hypoalbuminaemic state results in metabolic alkalosis. Production of urea (one way to compensate) is also impaired in patients with cirrhosis.

Bicarbonate loss due to ascites
Bicarbonate loss due to ascites with Bicarbonate loss due to ascites is incorrect. Ascites is associated with relative fluid depletionChat in the intravascular compartment, which actually drives an increase in bicarbonate.

Increased gastric acid production
Increased gastric acid production is incorrect. There is actually a reduction in 24-hour gastric acid secretion in patients with cirrhosis versus the general population.

Reduced bicarbonate secretion from the pancreas
Reduced bicarbonate secretion from the pancreas is incorrect. There is actually elevated output of water and bicarbonate from the pancreas in patients with cirrhosis, although the concentration of bicarbonate is reduced.

Reduced lactate formation in skeletal muscle
Reduced lactate formation in skeletal muscle is incorrect. Liver failure actually accentuates lactate formation rather than reducing it; reduced lactate formation does not significantly contribute to the alkalosis seen here.

stem: A 75-year-old woman is being followed by her GP for suspected developing primary hypothyroidism. She complains of tiredness all the time and has gained 3 kg in weight. On examination her BP is 132/82 mmHg, and pulse is 62 bpm and regular; her BMI is elevated at 32 kg/m 2. Which of the following biochemical changes would you most expect to be able to detect first?
explanation:
Increase in serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
In the early stages of hypothyroidism free thyroxine is maintained in the normal range by increased secretion of TSH. Patients with a slightly elevated TSH and low-normal thyroxine are said to have ‘compensated’ or ‘borderline’ hypothyroidism. In some individuals, it appears that this state can be maintained without progression to frank hypothyroidism.

Fall in serum free thyroxine (T4)
Fall in serum free thyroxine (T4) is incorrect. This occurs after increased levels of TSH can no longer maintain adequate output of thyroxine.

Fall in serum thyroxine-binding globulin
Chat Fall in serum thyroxine-binding globulin is incorrect. This tends to remain in the normal range in with patients with primary hypothyroidism.

Fall in serum free triiodothyronine (T3)
Fall in serum free triiodothyronine (T3) is incorrect. This occurs later than the fall in thyroxine for patients with primary hypothyroidism.

Fall in serum total triiodothyronine
Fall in serum total triiodothyronine is incorrect. Measurement of total thyroid hormones (free and bound fraction) is less sensitive than measuring the free hormones, and hence is likely to be seen last of all.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with nausea, vomiting and complaining of yellow visual field discoloration. On further questioning it transpires she has mixed up her tablets and been taking 250 mcg of digoxin per day for the last 2 weeks. Which of the following biochemical abnormalities, if present, would exacerbate her symptoms of digoxin poisoning?
explanation:
Hypokalaemia
Potassium depletion enhances the binding of digoxin to the Na +/K + pump. This increases the extent of inhibition of sodium transport, which can in turn cause digoxin toxicity. Correction of hypokalaemia is a key first step in management of the condition.

Hypocalcaemia
Hypocalcaemia is incorrect. This does cause QT prolongation, but it does not specifically impact on digoxin toxicity.

Hypermagnesaemia
Hypermagnesaemia with Hypermagnesaemia is incorrect. Magnesium is a co-factor for successful functioning of the Chat Na+/K+ pump, and low magnesium, therefore, exacerbates digoxin toxicity.

Hyponatraemia
Hyponatraemia is incorrect. Although this may worsen confusion, it does not increase the risk of cardiovascular manifestations of digoxin toxicity.

Hypophosphataemia
Hypophosphataemia is incorrect. Low phosphate does not exacerbate digoxin toxicity, although it is recognised to worsen cardiac failure by reducing left ventricular (LV) contractility.

stem: A 40-year-old female patient has been referred to hospital with jaundice. On examination, there is hepatosplenomegaly. She does not take any medication and does not drink alcohol. Her sister, who is 10 years older, had similar problems and has been diagnosed with a condition after antibody testing. Following serum testing, antibodies to which antigen are most likely to be detected in her serum?
explanation:
Anti-mitochondrial
The history is suggestive of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), an autoimmune condition where progressive destruction of the bile ducts in the liver occurs, leading to cholestasis, fibrosis and cirrhosis. Patients with primary biliary cholangitis are also at an increased risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma. Over 95% of patients with primary biliary cholangitis have antibodies to mitochondria (AMA), which are detectable in the serum before abnormalities in liver function are apparent and long before the onset of symptoms.

Anti-double-stranded DNA
Anti-double-stranded DNA is incorrect. These antibodies are diagnostic of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

Anti-histone Tutor of Anti-histone is incorrect. These auto-antibodies are found in the majority of patients with SLE and inAI >95% patients with drug-induced lupus.

Anti-transglutaminase
Anti-transglutaminase is incorrect. These antibodies are diagnostic of coeliac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis.

Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP)
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) is incorrect. These antibodies are diagnostic of rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: An 82-year-old woman has a calculated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 45 ml/min. Which of the following is likely to have the greatest impact on her measured estimated GFR (eGFR)?
explanation:
Muscle mass
Muscle mass has a strong impact on measurement of eGFR. In malnourished patients with low muscle mass, serum creatinine-based equations overestimate GFR. In patients with higher muscle mass, these equations underestimate GFR. In elderly patients, formal measurement of GFR may be considered in assessment of renal function.

Body fat percentage
Measured creatinine is not determined by body fat; it is determined by muscle mass, because creatinine is generated by protein turnover. Increased body fat may of course be associated with increased insulin resistance and hypertension, which can drive a worsening of renal function over time.

Carbohydrate intake
Carbohydrate intake is not a factor in assessment of eGFR because it has no impact on measured creatinine. Chat in with Over time, excess carbohydrate may be associated with incidental chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients without diabetes mellitus.

Fat intake
Higher intake of fat per se is not associated with worsening renal function over time. Higher intake of saturated fat has been shown in epidemiological studies to worsen albuminuria over time.

Protein intake
There is no evidence that changes in protein intake have an acute impact on renal function, and measured creatinine is most closely related to muscle mass, which is often reduced in the elderly. Patients with chronic excess protein consumption may be at increased risk of urate stone formation.

stem: A 64 year old woman who is treated with subcutaneous teriparatide for osteoporosis, comes to the clinic for review. She has now been taking the medication for 2 months. Which of the following is most useful in measuring the response to teriparatide?
explanation:
Procollagen type I N propeptide (PINP)
Teriparatide is a PTH analogue which increases osteoblast activity, as such measurement of bone formation markers is likely to be most useful in assessing response. Examples of markers of bone formation include: Procollagen type I propeptides C-terminal (PICP) N-terminal (PINP) Osteocalcin (OC)

Calcium
Calcium is incorrect. Calcium remains in the normal range in patients with osteoporosis. A fall may be seen in patients where osteoclast activity is inhibited, (e.g. with bisphosphonates or denosumab.

Cathepsin K
Cathepsin K is incorrect. Cathepsin K is a protease involved in bone resporption, as such it isn’t as useful as bone formation markers in assessing response to teriparatide.

C-terminal cross-linked telopeptide (CTX)
CTX is incorrect. C terminal telopeptide can be used as a marker of bone turnover, which is primarily elevated where there is increased bone reabsorption.

Tartrate resistant acid phosphatase.

stem: A 24-year-old woman undergoes resection of the terminal ileum with fashioning of an ileostomy for Crohn’s disease. Some 2 weeks after surgery, she is making a good recovery and is eating a high-energy, low-residue diet, but has a high ileostomy volume, necessitating intravenous fluid replacement. Her serum calcium concentration is 1.82 mmol/l, phosphate 1.28 mmol/l, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/l (normal < 150 U/l), albumin 30 g/l, creatinine 80 μmol/l. Prior to surgery, her corrected serum calcium concentration was 2.18 mmol/l and her albumin 36 g/l. What is the most likely cause of her hypocalcaemia?
options: Formation of insoluble calcium salts in the intestine
explanation:
Hypomagnesaemia
Patients with ileostomies can lose large amounts of magnesium through their stomas; hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion and can cause hypocalcaemia that is resistant to an increased provision of calcium. In this situation it’s important not only to replace calcium, but also to replace magnesium salts

Formation of insoluble calcium salts in the intestine
Formation of insoluble calcium salts in the intestine is incorrect. Impaired fat absorption can lead to the formation of insoluble calcium salts in the gut, although this isn’t relevant here because fat and calcium are predominantly absorbed in the proximal small intestine.

Hypoalbuminaemia
Hypoalbuminaemia is incorrect. Even with correction for hypoalbuminaemia, calcium is still low at approximately 2.0 mmol/l.

Malabsorption of calcium
Malabsorption of calcium is incorrect. Although some absorption of calcium occurs in the distal small intestine, most absorption of calcium occurs in the duodenum.

Malabsorption of vitamin D.

stem: A 56-year-old woman with known metastatic breast cancer presents to the Emergency Department with a calcium concentration of 3.22 mmol/l; her Cr is elevated at 195 mcmol/l and urea is 17.2 mmol/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Intravenous infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride
In this case there is significant evidence of dehydration, and rehydration with normal saline is the initial intervention of choice, establishing a diuresis which should promote calcium excretion.

Intravenous hydrocortisone
Intravenous hydrocortisone is incorrect. Corticosteroids have little impact in hypercalcaemia related to solid tumours.

Intravenous infusion of sodium phosphate
Intravenous infusion of sodium phosphate is incorrect. It is dangerous: it lowers the calcium concentration rapidly, but risks causing metastatic calcification.

Oral bisphosphonate
Oral bisphosphonate is incorrect. Their onset of action is too long to impact significantly on this patient’s hypercalcaemia.

Oral thiazide diuretic.

stem: An apparently healthy 20-year-old man has blood taken for lipid analysis in connection with an application for life insurance. He works as a builder and has no medical history of note. His body mass index (BMI) is 22 kg/m 2. The fasting triglyceride concentration is 4.0 mmol/l and HbA1C is 44 mmol/mol. He has no evidence of acanthosis nigricans on examination, and blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg. There is no family history of note although he admits to drinking alcohol in excess. As part of his work-up, he has an abdominal ultrasound which is reported as normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the hypertriglyceridaemia?
options: World Health Organisation (WHO) type 1 hyperlipidaemia (chylomicronaemia syndrome)
explanation:
A high alcohol intake
Alcohol consumption is a common cause of hypertriglyceridaemia, and all patients presenting with isolated hypertriglyceridaemia should be counselled on alcohol cessation or modification in combination with regular exercise, which can reduce triglyceride levels.

Undiagnosed diabetes mellitus
Undiagnosed diabetes mellitus is incorrect. This is very unlikely given the BMI, lack of family history and HbA1c level.

World Health Organisation (WHO) type 1 hyperlipidaemia (chylomicronaemia syndrome)
World Health Organization (WHO) type 1 hyperlipidaemia (chylomicronaemia syndrome) is incorrect. Chylomicronaemia syndrome is rare, usually presents in childhood and is associated with much higher triglyceride concentrations.

A high saturated fat intake
A high saturated fat intake is incorrect. A high saturated fat intake is more likely to elevate plasma cholesterol than triglyceride concentrations.

Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).

stem: A 22-year-old aid worker is admitted to the Emergency Department from the local airport; he apparently suffered from profuse watery diarrhoea during the flight and collapsed soon after walking from the plane. He has no past medical history of note. On examination his BP is 80/60 mmHg, pulse is 95 bpm and regular, he is severely dehydrated and has soiled himself during the ambulance journey. You suspect he has cholera. Which of the following is the mechanism by which cholera leads to fluid loss?
explanation:
GM1 receptor agonism
The answer is GM1-receptor agonism (Option D). Cholera endotoxin B subunits bind to the GM1 receptor located on small intestinal mucosa cells. Subsequent entry of the A1 subunit into secretory cells then leads to continuous adenylate cyclase activity, a sustained increase in cAMP and massive secretion of water and electrolytes into the small intestine.

GIP receptor antagonism
Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)-receptor antagonism (Option A) is incorrect. This is responsible for the second-phase insulin response, and is therefore a target for agonism in the treatment of Type 2 diabetes.

GLP1 receptor antagonism
GLP-1-receptor antagonism (Option B) is incorrect. This is an incretin, released in response to feeding, which leads to an increase in insulin release by beta cells in the pancreas; GLP-1 agonists are therefore used as a treatment for diabetes.

GLP2 receptor agonism
GLP-2-receptor agonism (Option C) is incorrect. This stimulates small intestine mucosal growth. For this reason, GLP-2 agonists are being developed for the treatment of radiotherapy-induced gastrointestinal damage and short bowel syndrome.

SGLT1 antagonism.

stem: A 24-year-old, unconscious man is admitted to the Emergency Department. No history is available. The results of arterial blood gas analysis are: pH 7.1, pCO 2 7.0 kPa, pO 2 8.2. HCO 3 - 17.1 mmol/l. These results indicate which one of the following acid–base disturbances?
explanation:
Mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis
The low pH in this patient indicates acidosis. The raised CO 2 and failure of the bicarbonate to rise (indeed it is below the lower limit of normal) indicates a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis.

Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation is incorrect. Respiratory compensation implies low pCO2, but the CO2 is in fact raised here, which does not fit with this proposed answer.

Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory acidosis is incorrect. Although the pCO2 is consistent with respiratory acidosis, the low bicarbonate fits with a mixed metabolic and respiratory picture.

Respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis is incorrect. The bicarbonate is below the lower limit of normal, which is inconsistent with a metabolic alkalosis.

Uncompensated metabolic acidosis.
